Reducing the number of AI use cases under consideration
Increasing the marketing budget

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fragmented data across legacy systems requires clear data ownership and integration before AI can use it effectively.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More sales reps: unrelated.
• Fewer use cases: doesn't fix data.
• More marketing: unrelated.

Key takeaway: integrate and own data first.

stem: Which statement best explains why establishing clear data ownership is important to an organization's AI strategy?

choices.text: Data ownership is only relevant to the physical storage hardware location
Ownership assigns accountability for data quality and use
Data ownership only matters for legal contracts and has no effect on AI model performance
Data ownership eliminates the need for any data governance policies

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clear ownership assigns accountability for data quality, access, and lifecycle, which AI initiatives depend on.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only physical storage: no.
• Only legal contracts: no.
• Eliminates governance: no.

Key takeaway: ownership = accountability for data.

stem: An organization plans to fine-tune a foundation model but discovers that its training data contains significant duplication, inconsistent labeling, and missing metadata. Compute budget is limited. What is the most effective use of the available budget?

choices.text: Immediately proceed with fine-tuning using the existing data to save time
Skip fine-tuning entirely and use only prompt engineering
Clean, deduplicate, and catalog the data first
Purchase additional GPU instances to fine-tune faster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning on messy data degrades results. Invest first in cleansing, deduplication, and metadata or cataloging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Proceed anyway: poor model.
• Skip entirely: may lose value.
• More GPUs: faster bad results.

Key takeaway: clean data before fine-tuning.

stem: After deploying a generative AI assistant company-wide, business units in different regions report inconsistent and sometimes biased responses. Investigation reveals each region trained on a different, disconnected extract of customer data with varying quality standards. Which foundational gap does this indicate?

choices.text: Excessive executive sponsorship in one region
Insufficient marketing localization
No unified data strategy or infrastructure
Too many employees trained in prompt engineering

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inconsistent results across regions point to the lack of a unified data strategy and consistent data infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Regional sponsorship: unlikely.
• Marketing localization: no.
• Too much training: no.

Key takeaway: consistent AI needs consistent data.

stem: A company preparing AI infrastructure must plan for model training spikes and connection to its ERP. What should it evaluate?

choices.text: Only the office Wi-Fi speed
Only the number of laptops per employee
Only the email system's storage quota
Compute, storage, network, and integration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AI infrastructure needs scalable compute and storage, adequate network throughput, and integration with existing systems such as ERP.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Wi-Fi, laptops, email: not AI infrastructure foundations.

Key takeaway: plan compute, storage, network, and integration together.

stem: A company wants one managed environment where data scientists prepare data, train, tune, and deploy custom ML models without managing servers. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker AI
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon QuickSight ML
Amazon Bedrock

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker AI covers the ML lifecycle for custom models: data prep, training, tuning, deployment, and monitoring.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bedrock: managed access to foundation models, not the full custom ML lifecycle.
• QuickSight: BI.
• DataBrew: data prep only.

Key takeaway: custom ML lifecycle → SageMaker AI.

stem: A readiness review produces two findings: Finding 1 states that customer records are inconsistently formatted across systems; Finding 2 states that current on-premises servers cannot scale to handle real-time inference workloads. How should these findings be classified?

choices.text: 1 is a data gap; 2 is a technology gap
Both findings are the same type of gap
Both findings are workforce culture gaps
Finding 1 is a technology gap; Finding 2 is a leadership gap

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inconsistent customer records are a data readiness gap. The second finding (about infrastructure or tooling) is a technology gap.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same type: no.
• Both culture gaps: no.
• Swapped categories: incorrect.

Key takeaway: classify gaps to target fixes.

stem: A large enterprise is deciding between a fully centralized data governance model, where one team owns all data policy decisions, and a decentralized model, where each business unit sets its own data standards. Which consideration most strongly supports centralizing at least core data ownership policies before scaling AI enterprise-wide?

choices.text: Decentralized ownership always produces higher quality data
Centralized ownership ensures consistent quality and standards
Business units never need access to their own data under a centralized model
Centralization eliminates the need for any data quality controls

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Centralized data governance helps ensure consistent quality and standards, but can slow business units' access and responsiveness.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Decentralized always higher quality: no.
• Units never need access: no.
• Removes quality controls: no.

Key takeaway: centralization trades agility for consistency.

stem: Two AI pilots failed because data was scattered, inconsistent, and owned by no one. Why is a data strategy foundational?

choices.text: It replaces the need for model evaluation
It decides which LLM vendor to buy
It makes the right data governed and accessible
It is only needed for regulatory reporting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A data strategy defines what data is collected, how it's governed and quality-controlled, and how it's made accessible, which reliable AI outputs depend on.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Vendor choice: separate.
• Replacing evaluation: models still need evaluation.
• Regulatory only: much broader.

Key takeaway: no data strategy, no reliable AI.

stem: A manufacturing company connected a new generative AI assistant to its internal document repository to speed up scaling of a pilot. Shortly after launch, employees discovered the assistant could surface confidential HR and legal documents to any employee who asked. Which foundational gap most directly caused this incident?

choices.text: Slow network bandwidth
Inadequate data access controls and governance during infrastructure setup
Insufficient marketing of the new tool
Lack of executive enthusiasm for AI

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An assistant exposing documents to the wrong people indicates inadequate data access controls and governance during integration.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bandwidth: no.
• Marketing: no.
• Executive enthusiasm: no.

Key takeaway: connect AI to data only with access controls.

stem: An enterprise's capability assessment finds that its on-premises data center lacks the elasticity to handle unpredictable spikes in inference traffic for a new customer-facing generative AI application. From a strategic infrastructure-foundation perspective, what is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Purchase a fixed number of additional on-premises servers sized for peak load year-round
Evaluate moving workloads to elastic cloud compute
Limit the application to a small pilot group indefinitely to avoid the issue
Discontinue the AI initiative entirely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lacking elastic compute, the company should evaluate moving relevant workloads to a cloud platform that scales on demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fixed servers: not elastic.
• Permanent small pilot: limits value.
• Discontinue: loses value.

Key takeaway: elastic AI workloads → cloud.

stem: An AI transformation stalls because departments won't share data or staff. What does executive sponsorship provide that fixes this?

choices.text: A guarantee of immediate ROI
Removal of all governance requirements
Commitment, resources, and alignment
Technical expertise to write the models

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Executive sponsors set priorities, allocate resources, and resolve cross-departmental conflicts, which technical teams can't do alone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Technical expertise: not the sponsor's role.
• Guaranteed ROI: unrealistic.
• Removing governance: harmful.

Key takeaway: sponsorship unblocks organizational barriers.

stem: A GenAI rollout team includes IT, legal, data science, HR, and business units. What is the main benefit of this mix?

choices.text: It removes the need for executive sponsorship
It speeds up every decision
Covers technical, legal, and people angles
It lowers the cost of model inference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Diverse perspectives reduce blind spots: legal catches compliance issues, HR handles workforce impact, business defines value, and IT ensures feasibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Faster decisions: more voices can slow decisions.
• Inference cost: unrelated.
• Sponsorship: still needed.

Key takeaway: cross-functional teams reduce blind spots.

stem: A logistics company's leadership wants to mandate immediate, company-wide adoption of a new AI-powered dispatch tool within two weeks, but a readiness survey shows deep skepticism among dispatchers who fear the tool will replace their judgment. What is the more effective approach to overcoming this cultural barrier?

choices.text: Quietly monitor dispatcher compliance without any communication
Engage dispatchers early through pilots and training
Cancel the AI initiative permanently due to the resistance
Mandate immediate full adoption without further discussion to save time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Engaging dispatchers early through pilots, training, and feedback builds trust and adoption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Silent monitoring: erodes trust.
• Cancel permanently: overreaction.
• Mandate without discussion: resistance.

Key takeaway: involve users to drive adoption.

stem: Employees' roles will shift as AI takes over routine tasks. Which workforce approach fits BEST?

choices.text: A single one-hour company-wide webinar
Replacing all affected staff with new hires
Waiting for employees to learn the new tools on their own
Targeted upskilling on AI literacy and new workflows

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Role-specific training on AI literacy and new workflows helps employees adopt tools and move into higher-value work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replace staff: costly and loses knowledge.
• Self-learning: uneven adoption.
• One webinar: too shallow.

Key takeaway: invest in role-specific upskilling.

stem: After deploying an AI system that automatically classifies incoming customer support tickets, a company redefines the role of its support agents to focus on reviewing edge cases the AI flags as low-confidence and handling escalations. What organizational change principle does this best illustrate?

choices.text: Reassigning agents to an unrelated department
Full automation with no human involvement
Shifting humans to oversight and exceptions
Complete elimination of the customer support function

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AI that handles classification shifts human roles from manual work to oversight, exceptions, and complex cases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Unrelated reassignment: no.
• Full automation with no humans: risky.
• Eliminate support: no.

Key takeaway: AI changes roles toward oversight.

stem: An AI transformation program has strong support from the Chief Technology Officer, but the Chief Operating Officer has not been engaged and continues to prioritize legacy process metrics that conflict with the new AI-driven workflows. Adoption has stalled across operations teams. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: Overly transparent communication
Insufficient computing infrastructure
Excessive employee training
Lack of aligned executive sponsorship across the leadership team

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Support from the CTO but not other executives shows a lack of aligned executive sponsorship across leadership.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Too transparent: no.
• Infrastructure: not indicated.
• Too much training: no.

Key takeaway: transformation needs aligned leadership.

stem: A company's AI adoption is slow even though tools are ready. Surveys show staff worry about job loss and distrust automated decisions. What is this, and what helps?

choices.text: A pricing barrier; negotiate lower model costs with vendors
A technical barrier; buy more compute
A data barrier; label more training data
A cultural barrier; communicate and involve employees

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fear and distrust are cultural barriers. Transparent communication, involving employees in design, and showing how AI augments their work build trust.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Compute, labeling, pricing: don't address fear or distrust.

Key takeaway: adoption is a people problem as much as a technology problem.

stem: During an AI transformation, which communication approach is more effective at surfacing and addressing employee concerns in real time?

choices.text: Communicating changes exclusively through the company's public press releases
Two-way channels such as town halls and feedback forums
One-way email announcements sent quarterly with no response mechanism
Restricting all AI-related communication to the legal department

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Two-way channels such as town halls and feedback forums surface concerns so leaders can address them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public website only: one-way.
• Quarterly emails: one-way.
• Legal only: excludes employees.

Key takeaway: two-way communication surfaces resistance.

stem: A company needs both AI technical expertise and organizational buy-in quickly, but has a limited budget. Which workforce approach best balances developing internal buy-in with building needed skills?

choices.text: Replace the entire existing workforce with newly hired AI specialists
Upskill existing staff, adding a few specialist hires
Avoid any hiring or training and hope employees learn AI skills unsupervised
Rely solely on external consultants for every AI task indefinitely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Upskilling motivated employees who know the business builds expertise and buy-in within a limited budget.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replace workforce: costly and disruptive.
• Hope employees learn: no plan.
• Consultants forever: no internal capability.

Key takeaway: upskill for skills and buy-in.

stem: An organization's leadership is designing a program to build an AI-ready workforce ahead of a major generative AI rollout. Select TWO elements that should be included in this program.

choices.text: Role-specific AI literacy training aligned to how jobs will change
A requirement that every employee become a certified machine learning engineer
A policy banning any employee discussion of AI outside official meetings
Clear communication about how employee roles and responsibilities will evolve
Immediate termination of roles most likely to be affected by automation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Role-specific AI literacy training and clear communication about how roles will change build an AI-ready workforce.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Everyone certified ML engineer: unrealistic.
• Ban discussion: harmful.
• Immediate terminations: harmful.

Key takeaway: prepare people for changing roles.

stem: Staff paste confidential data into unapproved public chatbots because they don't know an approved internal tool exists. What should the company do FIRST?

choices.text: Discipline employees who used public tools
Communicate the approved tool and rules
Block all AI tools, including the approved one
Stop the AI program until usage is controlled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The root cause is awareness. Proactive communication and training on the approved tool and guidelines steer usage to safe options, alongside technical controls for unapproved tools.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blocking everything: kills adoption.
• Discipline first: doesn't fix awareness.
• Stopping the program: loses value.

Key takeaway: shadow AI often means people don't know the approved path.

stem: A company successfully piloted a generative AI tool in one department and wants to scale it enterprise-wide. Which approach best reflects an iterative scaling methodology?

choices.text: Immediately deploying the tool to every department simultaneously without further testing
Limiting the tool permanently to the original pilot department
Expanding to a few departments, then refining
Waiting five years before considering any expansion

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Expanding to a few more departments, gathering feedback, and refining before a broader rollout scales safely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All at once: risky.
• Permanent limit: loses value.
• Wait five years: too slow.

Key takeaway: scale in phases.

stem: How does the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) differ from the AWS shared responsibility model in the context of enterprise AI transformation?

choices.text: CAF guides adoption; shared responsibility splits security duties
The shared responsibility model replaces the need for any organizational change management
They are identical frameworks with no meaningful difference
The AWS CAF only addresses billing, while the shared responsibility model only addresses marketing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The AWS CAF offers organizational perspectives (business, people, governance, platform, security, operations) for adoption. The shared responsibility model defines security duties between AWS and the customer.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replaces CAF: no.
• Identical: no.
• CAF only billing: no.

Key takeaway: CAF = adoption guidance; shared responsibility = security duties.

stem: Leadership at a bank is deciding whether to wait until an AI fraud-detection model achieves near-perfect accuracy before any deployment, or to deploy an already-effective model to a limited set of transactions now while continuing to improve it. Which approach better reflects recommended enterprise AI scaling practice?

choices.text: Wait indefinitely until the model is perfect before any deployment
Abandon the fraud-detection initiative since perfection is unattainable
Deploy to a limited scope now and improve iteratively
Deploy to all transactions immediately regardless of current performance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deploying an already-effective model to a limited scope now, with monitoring, delivers value while improving it iteratively.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Wait for perfection: never ships.
• Abandon: loses value.
• Deploy everywhere now: risky.

Key takeaway: ship useful models incrementally with safeguards.

stem: A generative AI proof of concept performed well in testing, but after being pushed directly into production without establishing monitoring, versioning, or rollback procedures, an unexpected model update caused inconsistent outputs that disrupted a customer-facing process. Which gap most directly caused this disruption?

choices.text: Lack of proper MLOps practices and business continuity safeguards during the transition from experimentation to production
Overinvestment in workforce training
Excessive executive sponsorship
Too much cross-functional collaboration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A PoC failing in production points to missing MLOps practices (testing, monitoring, deployment) and business continuity safeguards.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Too much training: no.
• Too much sponsorship: no.
• Too much collaboration: no.

Key takeaway: production needs MLOps.

stem: An AI pilot worked for 50 users, but problems appear as it scales to 5,000. Why are continuous feedback mechanisms important here?

choices.text: They replace the need for monitoring
They guarantee no new issues appear
They surface issues to improve iteratively
They are only useful during the pilot

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Feedback loops (user ratings, error reports, usage analytics) reveal issues that only appear at scale and guide improvements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replace monitoring: they complement it.
• Guarantee: nothing does.
• Pilot only: most valuable at scale.

Key takeaway: scale with feedback loops, not blind rollout.

stem: A business leader must choose a platform: one team needs a GenAI assistant using pretrained models quickly, another needs a custom churn model trained on company data. Which pairing fits?

choices.text: Bedrock for the assistant; SageMaker AI for churn
Bedrock for both, since it trains any custom model
SageMaker AI for both, since Bedrock has no models
SageMaker AI for the assistant; Bedrock for churn

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock provides managed API access to foundation models for GenAI apps. SageMaker AI covers building, training, and deploying custom ML models such as churn prediction.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: mismatched.
• Bedrock for everything: not a general custom ML training platform.
• No models in Bedrock: it hosts many foundation models.

Key takeaway: prebuilt GenAI → Bedrock; custom ML → SageMaker AI.

stem: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, when an organization fine-tunes a foundation model using Amazon Bedrock, which of the following is generally the customer's responsibility rather than AWS's?

choices.text: Patching the host operating system of the underlying managed service infrastructure
Physical security of the data centers hosting the underlying infrastructure
Maintaining the hardware that runs the foundation models
Fine-tuning data quality and governance, plus model access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Customers are responsible for the quality, appropriateness, and governance of their fine-tuning data and access configuration. AWS handles infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OS patching, physical security, hardware: AWS responsibilities.

Key takeaway: your data and configuration are your responsibility.

stem: An organization must decide whether to scale its successful AI use case by expanding it to additional departments with similar needs ('horizontal' scaling), or by deepening its capabilities within the original department ('vertical' scaling) before expanding elsewhere. Which factor should most influence this decision?

choices.text: The founding date of the company
Similarity of processes and data, and solution maturity
The number of press releases already issued about the pilot
The number of colors used in the AI application's user interface

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Expansion works best where business processes and data are similar across departments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Founding date, press releases, UI colors: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: scale where conditions match.

stem: A large enterprise discovers that five different business units have independently built nearly identical generative AI document-summarization tools, each using different vendors and standards, wasting resources. What structural change would most directly prevent this duplication going forward?

choices.text: Banning all AI projects company-wide
An AI Center of Excellence to coordinate standards
Removing all AI governance policies
Requiring each business unit to build even more independent tools

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An AI Center of Excellence coordinates standards, shares reusable components, and prevents duplicated effort across business units.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ban all AI: overreaction.
• Remove governance: worse.
• More independent builds: more duplication.

Key takeaway: reduce duplication → AI CoE.

stem: An AI claims triage system becomes mission critical. What business continuity measure is MOST important?

choices.text: Relying on the vendor's marketing claims of uptime
Removing all human reviewers to save cost
Fallback procedures and monitoring if the AI degrades
Deploying new versions without testing to move faster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mission-critical AI needs monitoring for outages and quality degradation, and fallback processes (manual or rules-based) so operations continue.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Removing reviewers: removes the fallback.
• Marketing claims: not a continuity plan.
• Untested releases: increase risk.

Key takeaway: plan for AI failure like any critical system.

stem: A company is preparing to transition a successful generative AI experiment into a production system used by thousands of employees. Select TWO practices that support a successful transition from experimentation to enterprise-grade production.

choices.text: Establishing monitoring, logging, and rollback procedures for the production system
Defining a business continuity plan for how operations continue if the AI system is unavailable
Restricting the system exclusively to the original pilot team indefinitely
Avoiding any documentation of the system's architecture or dependencies
Deleting all records of the original experimental results

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Production readiness needs monitoring, logging, and rollback procedures, and a business continuity plan for when the system fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Restrict to pilot team: not production.
• No documentation: risky.
• Delete experiment records: loses history.

Key takeaway: production = observability + continuity planning.

stem: An insurer has 25 proposed GenAI use cases and budget for three in the next year. Which prioritization approach is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Pick the three use cases with the most advanced technology.
Let each department build its own use case in parallel with no central criteria.
Start with the highest-risk customer-facing use case to maximize visibility.
Score use cases on value and feasibility; start high on both.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Score each use case on business value and feasibility (data readiness, risk, effort) and pick the top three.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Most advanced tech: not value-driven.
• Every department in parallel: exceeds budget.
• Highest-risk first: poor start.

Key takeaway: prioritize by value × feasibility.

stem: A logistics company needs to extract fields from standard invoices. This capability is widely available and not a source of competitive advantage. What sourcing approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Build and train a custom document model from scratch.
Hire a research team to publish papers on invoice extraction.
Postpone until a fully custom solution is possible.
Use a managed service or proven marketplace solution.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Invoice field extraction is a common, solved problem. A managed AWS AI service or proven marketplace solution delivers value fastest.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Build from scratch: slow.
• Research team: overkill.
• Wait for custom: delays value.

Key takeaway: commodity capabilities → buy, don't build.

stem: A company launches a GenAI assistant for contact-center agents. Six months later, leadership asks for ROI, but no one can show improvement. What was MOST likely missing?

choices.text: A higher token budget.
A larger model.
More prompt templates.
Baseline measurements of KPIs (such as handle time and first-contact resolution) captured before the pilot, with agreed targets.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Proving value requires baseline KPIs, such as handle time and first-contact resolution, measured before launch.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Token budget, larger model, more templates: don't prove value.

Key takeaway: no baseline, no proof of impact.

stem: A bank has run 12 GenAI pilots over 18 months, but none reached production. Which action BEST addresses this 'pilot purgatory'?

choices.text: Define production exit criteria up front and invest in shared platform, governance, and change management that make scaling repeatable.
Start 12 more pilots to increase the odds.
Stop all AI work.
Let each pilot team choose its own security review process.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Defining production exit criteria up front and investing in shared platforms and governance help pilots reach production.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More pilots: same problem.
• Stop all AI: overreaction.
• Each team's own security review: inconsistency.

Key takeaway: design pilots for production.

stem: A CFO asks for the total cost of ownership of a GenAI customer-support solution. Which TWO cost elements are MOST often underestimated? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Ongoing inference (token) costs that grow with adoption.
Data preparation, evaluation, monitoring, and human review operations.
Office furniture.
The price of the AWS console.
The one-time cost of a laptop for the project manager.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GenAI TCO includes ongoing inference (token) costs that grow with use, plus data preparation, evaluation, monitoring, and human review.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Furniture, console price, laptop: not meaningful AI costs.

Key takeaway: TCO includes usage and operational costs.

stem: An AI system recommends whether to deny loan applications. Which control is MOST important from a responsible AI perspective?

choices.text: Retrain the model daily.
Fully automate decisions to remove human bias.
Keep a human in the loop for adverse decisions, with explanations and an appeal process for applicants.
Hide the use of AI from applicants.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For adverse loan decisions, keep a human in the loop with explanations, supporting fairness and regulatory requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily retraining: not the key control.
• Full automation: removes oversight.
• Hide AI use: violates transparency.

Key takeaway: high-stakes decisions → human oversight + explanations.

stem: A multinational company wants a certifiable management system framework for governing AI across the organization, including policies, risk assessment, and continual improvement. Which standard fits BEST?

choices.text: ISO/IEC 27017 (cloud security controls).
ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management system).
ISO 9001 (quality management) only.
PCI DSS.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system standard for governing AI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ISO/IEC 27017: cloud security.
• ISO 9001: quality management.
• PCI DSS: payment cards.

Key takeaway: certifiable AI governance → ISO/IEC 42001.

stem: A company has dozens of AI systems across departments and no central view of where AI is used. Regulators are asking about high-risk uses. What should governance establish FIRST?

choices.text: A ban on all AI use.
An AI inventory with risk tiering of each system based on impact.
A hackathon to find new use cases.
A single model vendor for all use cases.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An AI inventory with risk tiering gives a central view of where AI is used and which systems need more oversight.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ban all AI: no.
• Hackathon: more use cases, not visibility.
• Single vendor: not visibility.

Key takeaway: govern what you can see → AI inventory.

stem: A retailer's customer-facing chatbot occasionally invents return policies. Leadership wants to reduce the business risk. Which combination is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Add a disclaimer and change nothing else.
Ground answers in approved policy documents (RAG), apply guardrails such as grounding checks, and escalate uncertain cases to human agents.
Use a bigger model and remove human agents.
Increase creativity settings.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Grounding answers in approved policy documents (RAG), applying guardrails, and routing uncertain cases to humans reduce invented policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disclaimer only: doesn't fix.
• Bigger model and no humans: riskier.
• More creativity: more invention.

Key takeaway: ground customer-facing answers.

stem: Employees fear that a new AI assistant will replace their jobs, and adoption is low. Which leadership action is MOST effective?

choices.text: Communicate the augmentation purpose clearly, involve employees in design, and provide role-based training and reskilling paths.
Mandate usage and track individual prompts.
Delay communication until the rollout is complete.
Limit access to senior managers.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Communicating the augmentation purpose, involving employees, and providing training address job fears and raise adoption.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Mandate and surveil: erodes trust.
• Delay communication: more fear.
• Limit to managers: excludes users.

Key takeaway: address fears transparently.

stem: Before committing to an AI strategy, a manufacturer realizes its maintenance data is spread across plants with inconsistent formats and unclear ownership. What should it do FIRST?

choices.text: Outsource the problem to a vendor with no data access.
Assess data readiness and fund the data groundwork.
Buy the largest available model.
Train a model on whatever data is easiest to obtain.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Assess data readiness first: quality, accessibility, ownership, and integration of the scattered maintenance data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Outsource without data: fails.
• Largest model: doesn't fix data.
• Easiest data: biased and incomplete.

Key takeaway: data readiness before strategy.

stem: Leadership worries about lock-in to a single foundation model provider as models evolve quickly. Which strategy BEST preserves flexibility?

choices.text: Build a foundation model in-house from scratch.
Use a multi-model platform behind an abstraction layer.
Sign a multi-year exclusive contract with one model provider.
Avoid GenAI until the market settles.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A platform offering multiple models through a common API (such as Bedrock) lets the company switch models as they evolve.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Build own FM: costly.
• Exclusive contract: lock-in.
• Avoid GenAI: loses value.

Key takeaway: reduce model lock-in → multi-model platform.

stem: GenAI spending grew 400% in a quarter, and finance cannot tell which business unit caused it. Which governance mechanism fits BEST?

choices.text: Move all workloads to one account without tags.
Cost allocation tagging (for example, per-application inference profiles), budgets with alerts, and a chargeback or showback model per business unit.
Ask teams to estimate their usage by email.
Cancel all GenAI subscriptions.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cost allocation tagging (for example, per application or business unit) makes GenAI spend attributable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One account without tags: less visibility.
• Email estimates: unreliable.
• Cancel everything: overreaction.

Key takeaway: attribute AI spend → tagging.

stem: Several competitors use the same public foundation models. Which factor is MOST likely to create a durable competitive advantage for a company's AI solutions?

choices.text: Publishing all internal data publicly.
Choosing the newest model every month.
Proprietary data, domain workflows, and customer relationships integrated into the AI solution.
Using the same prompts as competitors.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When everyone uses the same models, proprietary data, domain workflows, and customer relationships create differentiation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Publish data: gives away advantage.
• Newest model: easy to copy.
• Same prompts: no differentiation.

Key takeaway: differentiation comes from what others can't copy.

stem: A company plans to use AI for screening job applicants in multiple jurisdictions. Which governance approach is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Treat it like any low-risk internal tool.
Use it without telling candidates.
Classify it as high risk, conduct impact and bias assessments, document the system, ensure human oversight, and review applicable regulations in each jurisdiction.
Let the vendor handle all compliance obligations.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Applicant screening is high-risk in many jurisdictions. Classify it as such, conduct impact and bias assessments, and ensure transparency and oversight.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Low-risk treatment: noncompliant.
• Hide from candidates: noncompliant.
• Vendor handles everything: you remain accountable.

Key takeaway: hiring AI → high-risk governance.

stem: Using the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) for an AI transformation, which perspective primarily addresses workforce skills, culture, and organizational change?

choices.text: Platform perspective.
Operations perspective.
Security perspective.
People perspective.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The CAF People perspective covers culture, change management, skills, and organizational readiness.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Platform, Operations, Security: other concerns.

Key takeaway: workforce and change → People perspective.

stem: A customer-service GenAI assistant is launched. Which metrics BEST demonstrate business value to executives?

choices.text: Model parameter count.
Containment rate, customer satisfaction, and cost per resolved contact compared with baseline.
Number of engineers on the project.
Number of prompts sent and tokens consumed.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Containment rate, customer satisfaction, and cost per resolution show business value from a support assistant.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter count: technical.
• Engineer count: effort.
• Prompts and tokens: usage, not value.

Key takeaway: measure business outcomes, not activity.

stem: Under the shared responsibility model for a GenAI application on Amazon Bedrock, which responsibility belongs to the customer?

choices.text: App access, prompt data, guardrails, and output use.
Securing the physical data centers hosting the models.
Patching the hypervisors of the underlying infrastructure.
Maintaining the global network backbone.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
On Bedrock, the customer manages access to the application, the data sent in prompts, and how outputs are used. AWS secures infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Physical data centers, hypervisors, backbone: AWS responsibilities.

Key takeaway: your app, data, and access are yours to secure.

stem: A company new to GenAI must choose its first production use case. Which choice balances learning and risk BEST?

choices.text: An internal knowledge assistant with human review.
A fully autonomous customer-facing agent that issues refunds.
An AI system that sets prices for all products automatically.
A system that makes final medical diagnoses.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An internal knowledge assistant with human review offers real learning with limited risk for a first production use case.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Autonomous refunds: high risk.
• Automatic pricing: high risk.
• Final medical diagnoses: very high risk.

Key takeaway: start with lower-risk, high-learning use cases.

stem: A retailer's leadership asks why its new demand-forecasting model, trained on three years of sales, badly misjudged demand for a product line launched last month. The data team confirms the model worked as designed. What is the most likely explanation to give leadership?

choices.text: The model has no historical examples for the new product line, so its predictions for it are unreliable
Forecasting models only work for products that are sold in more than one region
The model needs a larger GPU instance to produce accurate forecasts for new product lines
The model should have been trained on fewer years of data so that it reflects only the most recent buying patterns

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A model learns patterns from the examples it was trained on. A product launched last month has almost no history, so the model is extrapolating beyond its training data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Forecasting models only work for products…: Region count is not a requirement for forecasting.
• The model needs a larger GPU instance to…: Compute size affects speed and cost, not what the model has learned.
• The model should have been trained on fewer…: Less history would weaken the patterns for existing products without fixing the gap for the new line.

Key takeaway: Models are only as good as the examples they learned from; new situations with little data need extra care.

stem: A bank's executive committee is choosing between two fraud models. Model X flags 95% of fraud but also flags many legitimate transactions. Model Y flags 70% of fraud with very few false alarms. Customer complaints about blocked cards are the board's top concern this year. How should the tradeoff be framed?

choices.text: Model X has higher recall but lower precision; Model Y favors precision, which reduces wrongly blocked cards
Model X has higher precision because it catches more fraud, while Model Y has higher recall and fewer misses
Model Y is overfitting because it flags fewer transactions, so its results cannot be trusted in production
Both models have the same overall accuracy, so the committee should decide based on licensing cost and vendor support alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Catching more of the real fraud is recall; being right when you raise a flag is precision. With complaints about blocked cards as the priority, Model Y's higher precision fits the goal, at the cost of missing more fraud.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model X has higher precision because it…: The terms are reversed: catching more of the fraud is recall, not precision.
• Model Y is overfitting because it flags…: Flagging fewer transactions reflects a threshold and precision choice, not overfitting.
• Both models have the same overall accuracy,…: The models clearly differ in errors, and accuracy alone hides the business tradeoff.

Key takeaway: Frame model choices in business terms: which error costs more, missed fraud or wrongly blocked customers.

stem: A product manager hears engineers say a chatbot's model is 'at inference' and asks what that stage means for the monthly budget. Which explanation is accurate?

choices.text: Inference is when the trained model answers real requests, so its cost grows with usage volume
Inference is the model evaluation step, so it runs only when the model changes
Inference is the one-time training run, so its cost is fixed once the model has been built and deployed
Inference is the data labeling phase, so its cost ends before launch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Training builds the model; inference is the model producing outputs for live requests. Inference cost scales with the number and size of requests, so it becomes an ongoing operating expense.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inference is the model evaluation step, so…: Evaluation measures quality; it does not serve users.
• Inference is the one-time training run, so…: That describes training, which usually happens before launch or periodically.
• Inference is the data labeling phase, so its…: Labeling prepares training data and is separate from serving requests.

Key takeaway: Training is mostly an upfront investment; inference is an ongoing cost that rises with adoption.

stem: An insurer wants to reduce time spent reading claim forms. Forms arrive as scanned PDFs, and adjusters need the policy number, incident date, and damage amount pulled into the claims system. Which type of AI solution fits this need?

choices.text: Document data extraction that reads scanned forms and returns structured fields
A recommendation system that suggests similar claims to adjusters
An image generation model that creates reference photos of damaged vehicles
A time-series forecasting model that predicts next month's claim volume for each region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The task is turning scanned documents into specific structured fields. Document extraction services such as Amazon Textract are built for that.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A recommendation system that suggests…: Recommendations suggest related items; they do not extract field values.
• An image generation model that creates…: Generating images does not read existing documents.
• A time-series forecasting model that…: Forecasting predicts volumes, not the contents of a single form.

Key takeaway: Match the AI solution type to the task: extracting fields from documents is a document-processing problem.

stem: A logistics company calculates shipping fees with a published rate table that regulators audit. A consultant proposes replacing the calculation with a machine learning model 'to modernize pricing.' What is the strongest reason to keep the rule-based calculation?

choices.text: A rule-based system learns new pricing patterns from historical shipment data faster than any machine learning model could
The fee must be exact, explainable, and reproducible from published rules, which a rule-based system already guarantees
Machine learning models always cost more to run than rule-based systems, regardless of volume or scale
Machine learning models are not permitted on cloud infrastructure in regulated industries such as logistics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When the answer is defined by fixed rules and must be exact and auditable, deterministic logic is the right tool. A model would add uncertainty without adding value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A rule-based system learns new pricing…: Rule-based systems do not learn at all; that is not their advantage here.
• Machine learning models always cost more to…: Cost depends on the workload; the deciding factor here is exactness and auditability.
• Machine learning models are not permitted on…: Machine learning runs in many regulated industries on AWS.

Key takeaway: Not every problem needs AI; exact, rule-defined, audited outcomes usually belong to deterministic logic.

stem: A call center wants to know, each day, which customer calls expressed frustration so supervisors can follow up. Calls are already transcribed to text. Which AI capability addresses this need most directly?

choices.text: Object detection on screenshots of the call center's live wallboard dashboard
Sentiment analysis on the transcripts to flag negative conversations
Speech synthesis to read transcripts aloud to supervisors
Machine translation of every transcript into three languages

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sentiment analysis classifies text by emotional tone, which directly identifies frustrated calls for follow-up. Services such as Amazon Comprehend provide it without building a model.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object detection on screenshots of the call…: Object detection works on images, not call content.
• Speech synthesis to read transcripts aloud…: Converting text to speech does not identify frustration.
• Machine translation of every transcript into…: Translation changes the language but does not measure tone.

Key takeaway: Name the business question first; here it is 'which calls were negative,' a sentiment task.

stem: An HR assistant built on a foundation model confidently cites a 'Section 7.4 remote work stipend' that does not exist in the company handbook. Employees are starting to rely on it. Which explanation and remedy should leadership understand?

choices.text: The handbook contains an error, so the policy team should add Section 7.4 to match the answer
The model generated plausible but false content, and grounding answers in retrieved handbook text reduces this risk
The model is too small; moving to a larger foundation model with more parameters will eliminate invented answers entirely
The model was hacked, and the only remedy is to rotate all employee passwords

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Foundation models can produce fluent content that is not true, often called hallucination. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in the actual handbook and can cite the source, which reduces invented details.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The handbook contains an error, so the…: Changing policy to match a mistake is backwards.
• The model is too small; moving to a larger…: Larger models still hallucinate; grounding and verification are the remedy.
• The model was hacked, and the only remedy is…: Invented content is a model behavior, not evidence of a breach.

Key takeaway: Plausible does not mean true; ground answers in approved sources and show citations.

stem: A marketing team wants its assistant to use the latest product catalog, which changes weekly. One vendor proposes fine-tuning a model every week; another proposes retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the catalog. Which statement best compares the options?

choices.text: RAG reads the current catalog at question time, while weekly fine-tuning adds retraining cost and still lags behind changes
RAG permanently updates the model's weights each week from the catalog, which makes it riskier and more expensive than fine-tuning
Both approaches are identical in cost and freshness, so the choice does not matter
Fine-tuning is the only way for a model to use company data, so RAG cannot answer catalog questions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RAG retrieves the relevant catalog entries when a question is asked, so answers reflect the latest data without retraining. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into the model and must be repeated as data changes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RAG permanently updates the model's weights…: RAG does not change model weights; fine-tuning does.
• Both approaches are identical in cost and…: They differ substantially in cost, effort, and how current the answers are.
• Fine-tuning is the only way for a model to…: RAG is a common way to use company data without training.

Key takeaway: For frequently changing facts, retrieve at question time instead of retraining.

stem: A legal team notices its drafting assistant produces different clause wording every time for the same request, while the marketing team wants more variety in ad copy. Which model setting explains both observations?

choices.text: Temperature, which controls how random or varied the generated output is
Maximum tokens, which controls how factual and well sourced the model's answers are
Embedding size, which controls how quickly the model returns each generated response
Context window, which controls how many users can send requests to the model at the same time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lower temperature makes outputs more consistent and predictable, which suits legal drafting; higher temperature adds variety, which suits creative copy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Maximum tokens, which controls how factual…: Maximum tokens limits output length, not factual accuracy.
• Embedding size, which controls how quickly…: Embedding size relates to vector representations, not response variety.
• Context window, which controls how many…: The context window is how much text the model can consider, not user concurrency.

Key takeaway: Tune temperature to the task: low for consistency, higher for creativity.

stem: A company wants an assistant that can check an order's status, issue a refund under $50, and email the customer, deciding which step to take based on the conversation. Which capability distinguishes this from a basic chatbot?

choices.text: A faster model so the chatbot replies to every customer message in under one second
An agent that plans steps and calls tools or APIs to act on the customer's behalf
A larger context window so the chatbot can read longer customer messages and full order histories in a single turn
A translation layer so the chatbot can answer customers in more languages

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Acting on systems (checking orders, issuing refunds, sending emails) and choosing which action to take requires an agent that can plan and call tools, with guardrails on what it may do.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A faster model so the chatbot replies to…: Speed improves experience but not the ability to act.
• A larger context window so the chatbot can…: Reading longer messages does not let it take actions.
• A translation layer so the chatbot can…: Languages broaden reach but do not add actions.

Key takeaway: Agents turn answers into actions; define their tools and limits carefully.

stem: A board member asks why a model that scored 99% on the data it was trained on scored only 64% on new customer data. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: The 99% score proves the model is correct and the new data is mislabeled
The model memorized its training data instead of learning patterns that generalize, which is overfitting
The model was underfitting, meaning it was too simple to learn the patterns in the training data
New customer data is always lower quality than training data, so any model will score far lower on it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A large gap between training performance and performance on new data is the classic sign of overfitting: the model fit noise and specifics of the training set.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The 99% score proves the model is correct…: High training accuracy says nothing about generalization.
• The model was underfitting, meaning it was…: Underfitting shows poor results on training data too, not 99%.
• New customer data is always lower quality…: Lower scores on new data are not automatic; a large gap signals a modeling problem.

Key takeaway: Judge models on data they have not seen; a big train-versus-test gap means overfitting.

stem: A mid-sized retailer wants product recommendations on its website within one quarter. It has two data scientists and clean purchase history. Which approach best balances speed and fit for this business?

choices.text: Build a custom recommendation algorithm from research papers before launch
Wait until the team has five years of data before starting any recommendations
Use a managed recommendation service trained on its own purchase data
Use a general-purpose chatbot to write product suggestions for each visitor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A managed service such as Amazon Personalize provides proven recommendation algorithms trained on the company's own data, fitting a small team and a one-quarter timeline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Build a custom recommendation algorithm from…: Building from research is slow and risky for a two-person team.
• Wait until the team has five years of data…: Existing clean purchase history is already enough to start.
• Use a general-purpose chatbot to write…: A chatbot is not designed to rank products from behavior data.

Key takeaway: When speed matters and the problem is common, managed AI services beat custom builds.

stem: A support team pastes the full 300-page policy manual into every prompt, and costs doubled while answers got slower. Which changes address both problems while keeping answers accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Cache the stable instructions and reference text that repeat across prompts
Remove the policy manual entirely and rely on the model's general knowledge
Raise the model temperature so answers are generated faster
Switch to a model with a larger context window and keep sending the full manual with every customer question
Retrieve only the relevant manual sections for each question instead of sending the whole manual

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cost and latency grow with the number of tokens processed. Retrieving only relevant sections cuts tokens per request, and prompt caching avoids reprocessing repeated content, while both keep answers grounded in the manual.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove the policy manual entirely and rely…: Dropping the manual removes the grounding the answers need.
• Raise the model temperature so answers are…: Temperature changes variety, not speed or cost.
• Switch to a model with a larger context…: A larger context window still processes the whole manual on every request.

Key takeaway: Send the model only what it needs, and reuse what repeats.

stem: A healthcare startup is preparing training data for a model that triages patient messages. Which TWO data issues most threaten the model's usefulness? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Training data kept in Amazon S3 instead of an on-premises server
Training data drawn almost entirely from one clinic's patient population
Labels written in lowercase letters instead of title case
Messages stored as UTF-8 text files in a shared folder instead of as scanned PDF documents
Messages labeled inconsistently by different reviewers for the same symptoms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inconsistent labels teach the model conflicting answers, and data from one population may not represent other patients, causing poor or biased results elsewhere.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Training data kept in Amazon S3 instead of…: Where data is stored does not change its quality.
• Labels written in lowercase letters instead…: Label casing is cosmetic and easy to normalize.
• Messages stored as UTF-8 text files in a…: Plain text is a convenient format for training.

Key takeaway: Label quality and representativeness matter more than format or storage location.

stem: A publisher wants an assistant to answer questions in its house style using its archive of 20,000 edited articles. Style must be consistent, but facts must reflect the latest editions. Which combination fits best? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Increase the maximum output tokens so answers include more facts
Use retrieval over the current article archive so facts stay up to date
Rely on prompt instructions alone and never provide any article content to the model at query time
Retrain a model from scratch on the publisher's archive alone
Fine-tune a model on edited articles to teach the house style

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning shapes tone and style consistently, while retrieval supplies current facts at question time. Together they address style and freshness.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the maximum output tokens so…: Longer outputs do not make facts more current.
• Rely on prompt instructions alone and never…: Instructions alone cannot supply current facts.
• Retrain a model from scratch on the…: Training from scratch needs far more data and cost than 20,000 articles justify.

Key takeaway: Fine-tune for how to say it; retrieve for what is currently true.

stem: A regional bank has 14 proposed AI projects and budget for three this year. The CEO asks for a way to choose that the board will accept. Which prioritization approach is most defensible?

choices.text: Fund the three projects that use the most advanced AI techniques, since those create the strongest market perception of innovation
Start with the three cheapest projects so the bank can show quick spending discipline to the board members
Score each project on expected business value, feasibility with current data and skills, and risk, then pick the top three
Let each department vote, and fund the three projects that receive the most internal votes this quarter

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A value-feasibility-risk matrix ties each project to measurable outcomes and realistic delivery, which gives the board a transparent reason for each choice.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fund the three projects that use the most…: Technical novelty is not a business outcome and often raises risk.
• Start with the three cheapest projects so…: Low cost alone ignores whether a project delivers anything.
• Let each department vote, and fund the three…: Votes measure enthusiasm, not value or feasibility.

Key takeaway: Prioritize AI initiatives by value, feasibility, and risk together, not by novelty, popularity, or price.

stem: A support organization launched an AI assistant that drafts replies for agents. Leadership wants proof of value after 90 days. What must have been captured before launch for that proof to be credible?

choices.text: The number of prompts the development team tested while building the assistant during its pilot phase
A survey of executives asking how much value they expect the assistant to create over the next year
Baseline metrics such as average handling time and resolution rate from before the assistant was introduced
The list of foundation models evaluated during vendor selection, along with their published benchmark scores

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Value is shown as change against a starting point. Without pre-launch baselines for the target metrics, improvements after launch cannot be attributed or quantified.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of prompts the development team…: Prompt counts describe development effort, not business impact.
• A survey of executives asking how much value…: Expectations are not measurements.
• The list of foundation models evaluated…: Benchmarks describe models, not results in this organization.

Key takeaway: Measure the baseline before launch, or you cannot prove the change afterward.

stem: An AI invoice-processing tool cost $400,000 to deploy and $100,000 a year to run. It saves 12,000 staff hours a year at a loaded cost of $50 per hour. Which statement about the first-year return is accurate?

choices.text: Annual savings are $120,000, so the tool will not break even for more than four years under current assumptions
The tool loses money in year one because staff hours saved cannot be converted into dollars for a business case
Annual savings are $600,000, so the first year returns $500,000 net because deployment is a one-time cost
Annual savings are $600,000, so the first year returns about $100,000 net after deployment and running costs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Savings are 12,000 hours times $50, or $600,000. Subtracting the $400,000 deployment and $100,000 running cost leaves about $100,000 net in year one, with later years netting $500,000.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Annual savings are $120,000, so the tool…: 12,000 times $50 is $600,000, not $120,000.
• The tool loses money in year one because…: Loaded hourly cost is a standard way to value time saved.
• Annual savings are $600,000, so the first…: One-time costs still count against the year they are incurred.

Key takeaway: Include one-time and recurring costs when stating first-year return, and show later years separately.

stem: A mid-sized insurer wants AI-assisted claims triage within six months. It has strong claims data, two ML engineers, and no plan to sell AI products. Which sourcing approach best fits?

choices.text: Delay the initiative until the insurer can hire a research team of twenty scientists for custom development
Buy a closed third-party product that cannot use the insurer's own data, to avoid any integration work
Build on managed AWS AI services using its own claims data, rather than developing models from scratch
Develop a proprietary foundation model from scratch so the insurer fully owns every layer of the technology

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed services give a small team a fast path while still using the insurer's differentiating data, balancing speed, cost, and fit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delay the initiative until the insurer can…: Waiting sacrifices the six-month goal without a clear benefit.
• Buy a closed third-party product that cannot…: Ignoring its own data throws away the insurer's advantage.
• Develop a proprietary foundation model from…: Building a foundation model is far beyond the timeline, team, and need.

Key takeaway: Build on managed services when speed matters and your advantage is your data, not the model itself.

stem: Two competitors deploy the same public foundation model for customer service. One consistently outperforms the other in customer satisfaction. Which factor most likely explains the difference?

choices.text: The better-performing company runs the model in a different AWS Region that has newer data centers and hardware
The better-performing company renamed the assistant with a friendlier brand name that customers remember more easily
The better-performing company pays a higher per-token price for the same model, which improves its answer quality
Integration with its own customer history, product data, and support workflows that the other company lacks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When models are the same, differentiation comes from proprietary data, workflow integration, and customer context that competitors cannot copy easily.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The better-performing company runs the model…: Region choice affects latency and compliance, not answer quality.
• The better-performing company renamed the…: Branding may help adoption but does not make answers better.
• The better-performing company pays a higher…: The same model at a different price produces the same outputs.

Key takeaway: Durable advantage comes from your data and processes, not from access to a common model.

stem: A retail COO wants 'an AI strategy' after a competitor announced a chatbot. What should come first when shaping the strategy?

choices.text: Hire a chief AI officer and wait for that person to decide which departments should use AI at all
Launch a chatbot within 30 days so the company matches the competitor's announcement as quickly as possible
Identify the business outcomes the company most needs to improve and where AI could plausibly help
Select the most capable foundation model on the market and license it before defining any use cases

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A strategy starts from business goals and pain points, then evaluates where AI is a good fit. Starting from a tool or a competitor's move risks solving the wrong problem.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hire a chief AI officer and wait for that…: Leadership structure matters, but waiting does not define outcomes.
• Launch a chatbot within 30 days so the…: Copying a competitor is reactive and may not fit the retailer's needs.
• Select the most capable foundation model on…: Choosing a model before a use case reverses the logic.

Key takeaway: Start AI strategy with the business outcomes you need, not the technology or the competition.

stem: A marketing team reports that its AI content tool 'generated 4,000 articles this quarter.' The CFO is unimpressed. Which metric would better show business value?

choices.text: The number of employees who logged in to the tool at least once during the quarter under review
The number of prompts marketers wrote each week while using the tool to generate the articles
The average word count of generated articles compared with the articles the team wrote by hand last year
Change in qualified leads or conversions attributed to the content compared with the prior baseline

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Output volume is an activity metric. Business value is shown by outcomes the content drives, such as qualified leads or conversions against a baseline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of employees who logged in to the…: Logins measure adoption, not value.
• The number of prompts marketers wrote each…: Prompt counts measure effort, not results.
• The average word count of generated articles…: Word count says nothing about impact.

Key takeaway: Report outcome metrics tied to business goals, not activity or usage counts.

stem: A hospital network is choosing its first generative AI initiative. Option 1 summarizes internal meeting notes. Option 2 drafts patient discharge instructions sent directly to patients. Both have similar projected value. Which reasoning best guides the first choice?

choices.text: Start with meeting summaries, which carry lower risk and let the organization build skills and governance first
Start with discharge instructions, because patient-facing use cases always produce the fastest return on investment
Start with neither until regulators publish rules specific to generative AI in every jurisdiction the network serves
Start with both at once, because running two pilots in parallel always halves the time to enterprise adoption

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With similar value, a lower-risk internal use case lets the organization learn, set up governance, and prove results before exposing patients to AI-generated content.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Start with discharge instructions, because…: Patient-facing content carries higher safety and regulatory risk, and faster return is not guaranteed.
• Start with neither until regulators publish…: Waiting for complete regulation stalls learning indefinitely.
• Start with both at once, because running two…: Parallel pilots do not halve time and double the governance load.

Key takeaway: When value is similar, choose the lower-risk use case first to build capability and trust.

stem: A company wants to judge whether its AI sales assistant, not a seasonal upturn, caused a 9% rise in win rates. Which evaluation design gives the most credible answer?

choices.text: Count how many proposals the assistant drafted, and assume each drafted proposal produced one additional win
Compare a group of sales reps using the assistant with a similar group not using it over the same period
Ask the sales reps using the assistant whether they believe it helped them close more deals this quarter
Compare this quarter's win rate with the same quarter five years ago, before any AI tools were in use

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A concurrent control group experiences the same season and market, so the difference between groups isolates the assistant's effect.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Count how many proposals the assistant…: Drafted proposals are activity, and assuming each became a win is unfounded.
• Ask the sales reps using the assistant…: Self-reports are biased and not measured outcomes.
• Compare this quarter's win rate with the…: Five-year-old results differ in many ways besides AI.

Key takeaway: Use a control group to separate AI impact from market and seasonal effects.

stem: A company worries about lock-in to one foundation model provider as models improve quickly. Which approach best preserves flexibility without slowing delivery?

choices.text: Build applications against a platform that offers several models through a common API, and keep prompts and evaluations portable
Sign a five-year exclusive contract with the current leading provider in exchange for a volume discount
Build every application on a different model provider so that no single provider ever handles more than one workload at a time
Avoid foundation models entirely until the market consolidates around a single long-term technology leader

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A multi-model platform such as Amazon Bedrock plus portable prompts and evaluation sets lets the company switch models as they evolve without rewriting applications.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sign a five-year exclusive contract with the…: An exclusive long contract increases lock-in.
• Build every application on a different model…: Scattering providers adds complexity and inconsistency without real portability.
• Avoid foundation models entirely until the…: Waiting forgoes value while the market keeps moving.

Key takeaway: Reduce lock-in with an abstraction layer and portable assets, not by avoiding or scattering providers.

stem: A logistics firm's AI pilot met its technical goals, but executives disagree on whether to scale it. Which artifact would best support a go or no-go decision?

choices.text: A detailed architecture diagram showing every AWS service the pilot used during its three months of testing
A press release draft announcing the pilot's success to customers and investors ahead of the final decision
A business case comparing measured pilot results with the costs, risks, and resources required to scale
A list of all the prompts and model settings the team experimented with while tuning the pilot's outputs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scaling decisions weigh demonstrated value against the full cost, risk, and effort of expansion; a business case built on pilot measurements makes that comparison explicit.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A detailed architecture diagram showing…: Architecture detail supports engineering, not the investment decision.
• A press release draft announcing the pilot's…: Announcing before deciding creates pressure without evidence.
• A list of all the prompts and model settings…: Tuning history is technical detail.

Key takeaway: Decide on scaling with measured results versus full scaling costs and risks.

stem: A company is choosing KPIs for an AI document-review tool used by its legal team. Which pair combines an efficiency measure with a quality measure?

choices.text: Number of pages processed per week and the average page count of contracts reviewed by the tool
Monthly model inference cost and the number of different model versions tested during the quarter
Number of contracts uploaded to the tool and the number of lawyers with active user accounts
Review time per contract and the rate of issues missed that were later found by senior lawyers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Review time captures efficiency, and the missed-issue rate captures quality. Tracking both prevents speed gains that quietly reduce accuracy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Number of pages processed per week and the…: Both are volume measures.
• Monthly model inference cost and the number…: Cost matters, but model versions tested is not a quality outcome.
• Number of contracts uploaded to the tool and…: These measure usage, not efficiency or quality.

Key takeaway: Pair speed or cost KPIs with quality KPIs so improvements are real.

stem: A software vendor considers partnering with a specialized AI firm instead of building a capability in-house. When is a partnership the strongest choice?

choices.text: When the vendor wants to avoid defining any requirements and prefers the partner to decide the business goals
When the capability is needed soon, is not a core differentiator, and the partner has proven expertise the vendor lacks
When the capability is the vendor's main source of competitive advantage and must remain entirely proprietary
When the vendor already has a large, experienced in-house team that has built and operated the same capability successfully before

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partnering fits needs that are time-sensitive and not core, where the partner brings expertise the company does not have. Core differentiators are usually worth building.

Why the other options are wrong:
• When the vendor wants to avoid defining any…: Handing over business goals is poor governance, not a partnership strategy.
• When the capability is the vendor's main…: Core differentiators are usually kept in-house.
• When the vendor already has a large,…: Existing in-house expertise favors building.

Key takeaway: Build what differentiates you; buy or partner for what is urgent and non-core.

stem: A manufacturer's AI steering committee wants a balanced portfolio of AI initiatives. Which TWO practices support that goal? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Choose initiatives mainly by which AI techniques are newest, to keep the company's reputation for innovation
Review each initiative regularly and pause or stop those that miss agreed milestones
Approve only initiatives that require no new data collection, so work can start the week they are approved
Fund every proposal equally so that no department feels its ideas were treated unfairly by the committee
Mix quick, low-risk wins with a smaller number of longer-term initiatives that could create larger advantages

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A balanced portfolio combines near-term wins that build credibility with bets that could pay off more, and regular reviews redirect money from initiatives that are not delivering.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Choose initiatives mainly by which AI…: Newness is not a business criterion.
• Approve only initiatives that require no new…: Excluding any data work rules out many valuable initiatives.
• Fund every proposal equally so that no…: Equal funding ignores value and risk.

Key takeaway: Balance near-term and long-term bets, and prune initiatives that miss milestones.

stem: A company's AI assistant cut average call time by 20%, but the CFO sees no reduction in cost. Which TWO follow-up questions best explain whether value is being realized? (Select TWO)

choices.text: How many tokens did the assistant use per call compared with the vendor's advertised average usage?
Which foundation model version was used, and has the vendor released a newer version since launch?
Did customer satisfaction or first-contact resolution change, since faster calls might hurt or help quality?
How many employees attended the assistant's launch training session and completed the online course?
Was the freed agent time redirected to other work, or did staffing and workload plans stay unchanged?

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Time saved only becomes value when it is redeployed or reduces cost, and speed gains must be checked against quality outcomes that also drive value.

Why the other options are wrong:
• How many tokens did the assistant use per…: Token usage explains cost of the tool, not realized business value.
• Which foundation model version was used, and…: Model version is a technical detail unrelated to the gap.
• How many employees attended the assistant's…: Training attendance measures enablement, not value.

Key takeaway: Efficiency gains become value only when capacity is redeployed and quality holds.

stem: A bank evaluates an AI solution from AWS Marketplace. Which TWO considerations matter most before committing? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Whether the vendor's marketing materials use the same terminology as the bank's internal documents
The number of other products the vendor lists on AWS Marketplace across unrelated industries
The color scheme of the vendor's user interface compared with the bank's corporate brand colors
The contract terms for data use, exit, and portability if the bank later changes providers
Whether the solution can work with the bank's data under its security and compliance requirements

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fit with the bank's data and compliance obligations determines whether the solution can be used at all, and data and exit terms determine lock-in and risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whether the vendor's marketing materials use…: Terminology can be aligned later.
• The number of other products the vendor…: Catalog size says little about this solution's fit.
• The color scheme of the vendor's user…: Visual style is cosmetic.

Key takeaway: For bought AI, check data, security, and compliance fit, plus exit and portability terms.
