stem: Finance asks whether to report an AI project's value as 'hours saved' or 'dollars saved.' The saved hours are being reassigned to new customer outreach rather than reducing headcount. Which reporting approach is most accurate?

choices.text: Report hours redeployed and the outcomes of the new outreach, rather than claiming a direct cost reduction
Report the vendor's advertised savings figure, since it was calculated from many customers' deployments
Report nothing until headcount is reduced, since value only counts when salaries are removed from the budget
Report the full dollar value of the saved hours as a cost reduction, even though payroll costs did not change

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When saved time is redeployed, the honest story is capacity freed and what that capacity achieved, not a cost reduction that did not occur.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Report the vendor's advertised savings…: Vendor averages are not this company's measured results.
• Report nothing until headcount is reduced,…: Redeployed capacity can create real value without cutting staff.
• Report the full dollar value of the saved…: Claiming unrealized cost cuts misstates financial impact.

Key takeaway: Report value in the form it was actually realized: cost reduction or redeployed capacity and its outcomes.

stem: A company's AI roadmap lists initiatives but no owners, timelines, or success measures. What is the most important improvement to make the roadmap actionable?

choices.text: Assign an accountable business owner, a timeline, and measurable success criteria to each initiative
Remove all timelines so teams can experiment freely without pressure to show results by a certain date
Add more initiatives to the roadmap so that every department has at least one AI project assigned to it
Replace the roadmap with a list of AI vendors the company has already met during the past year

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Ownership, timing, and measurable outcomes turn a list of ideas into a plan that can be tracked and governed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all timelines so teams can experiment…: Removing timelines reduces accountability.
• Add more initiatives to the roadmap so that…: More initiatives dilute focus.
• Replace the roadmap with a list of AI…: A vendor list is not a plan.

Key takeaway: Every AI initiative needs an owner, a timeline, and success measures.

stem: A fashion retailer has 15 years of detailed customer style preferences and returns data. How can this asset create a durable competitive advantage with generative AI?

choices.text: Delete older data because generative AI models only need the most recent few months of customer information
Use the proprietary data to personalize recommendations and content in ways competitors using public data cannot copy
Sell the raw customer data to competitors so the whole industry benefits from better generative AI models
Publish the data openly so foundation model providers include it in their next public model training runs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Proprietary data that competitors lack is a key source of differentiation; applied to personalization, it produces experiences others cannot easily match.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete older data because generative AI…: Long history can be valuable for preferences and returns patterns.
• Sell the raw customer data to competitors so…: Selling the asset gives away the advantage and raises privacy concerns.
• Publish the data openly so foundation model…: Publishing the data hands it to everyone.

Key takeaway: Proprietary data is a lasting differentiator when AI puts it to work.

stem: A company's AI chatbot deflected 40% of support contacts, yet support costs rose. Investigation shows customers often call after unhelpful chatbot answers. What does this reveal about the chosen KPI?

choices.text: Support costs cannot be linked to chatbot performance, so no KPI can ever capture the chatbot's real business value
The chatbot should deflect even more contacts, since higher deflection always lowers total support costs
Deflection rate is the correct KPI, and the cost increase must be caused by unrelated seasonal factors
Deflection rate alone ignored resolution, so failed conversations created repeat contacts that raised costs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deflection counts contacts the chatbot handled, not whether customers' problems were solved. Unresolved conversations came back as calls, so a resolution-based KPI is needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Support costs cannot be linked to chatbot…: Resolution and repeat-contact rates do link chatbot quality to cost.
• The chatbot should deflect even more…: Deflecting without resolving creates more repeat contacts.
• Deflection rate is the correct KPI, and the…: The investigation directly links the calls to chatbot failures.

Key takeaway: Measure outcomes such as resolution, not proxies such as deflection, or the KPI can hide failure.

stem: A lender's AI credit model approves applicants from one postal region at a much lower rate than others with similar finances. The model does not use region as an input. What is the most likely cause, and the right first step?

choices.text: The gap proves the training data was stolen or tampered with, so the model should be retired and the incident reported to police
The model is working as intended, since lenders are allowed to use any statistically predictive pattern
Other inputs act as proxies for region, so the team should measure outcomes by group and investigate those features
The model cannot be biased because region is not an input, so the approval gap must be a reporting error

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Removing a sensitive attribute does not remove bias; correlated features such as address history or income patterns can act as proxies. Measuring outcomes across groups and examining those features is the right start.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The gap proves the training data was stolen…: Bias is a fairness issue, not evidence of theft.
• The model is working as intended, since…: Predictive patterns can still be unfair or unlawful.
• The model cannot be biased because region is…: Proxies can reproduce bias without the attribute itself.

Key takeaway: Test outcomes across groups; excluding a sensitive attribute does not guarantee fairness.

stem: A company tells customers when they are chatting with an AI assistant and explains what data the assistant uses. Which responsible AI principle does this primarily support?

choices.text: Robustness, so the assistant keeps working correctly when inputs are unusual or noisy
Veracity, so every answer the assistant gives is guaranteed to be factually correct
Transparency, so users understand when AI is involved and how it reaches its outputs
Controllability, so administrators can shut the assistant down during an emergency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Disclosing AI involvement and the data used helps people understand and calibrate their trust, which is the core of transparency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Robustness, so the assistant keeps working…: Robustness concerns reliable behavior under varied inputs.
• Veracity, so every answer the assistant…: Veracity aims for accuracy, but disclosure does not guarantee correctness.
• Controllability, so administrators can shut…: Controllability concerns oversight and intervention.

Key takeaway: Telling users when AI is involved and what it uses is transparency.

stem: A European retailer plans an AI system that screens job applicants. Which governance step should happen before deployment?

choices.text: A decision to keep the system's use secret from applicants so that candidates cannot game the screening
A documented risk assessment covering fairness, human oversight, and applicable regulations for high-impact uses
A contract clause stating that the software vendor alone is legally responsible for any unfair outcomes
A marketing plan announcing that hiring decisions will soon be fully automated, to attract more applicants to open roles

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hiring decisions significantly affect people and are treated as high risk under regulations such as the EU AI Act. A documented assessment of fairness, oversight, and legal requirements belongs before launch.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A decision to keep the system's use secret…: Secrecy conflicts with transparency obligations.
• A contract clause stating that the software…: Deploying organizations keep accountability for how they use AI.
• A marketing plan announcing that hiring…: Announcing full automation raises risk rather than managing it.

Key takeaway: High-impact AI uses need a documented risk and compliance assessment before deployment.

stem: A company has 30 teams experimenting with generative AI and no common rules. Leadership wants consistency without stopping innovation. Which governance structure fits best?

choices.text: A rule that only the IT department may use generative AI, with every other team required to submit tickets for each request
A complete ban on generative AI until an external auditor certifies every possible future use case
No central policy, so each team can decide its own rules according to the needs of its own customers
A cross-functional AI governance group that sets shared policies and risk tiers while teams build within them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A cross-functional group with clear policies and risk-based review sets guardrails while letting teams move quickly on lower-risk work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A rule that only the IT department may use…: Centralizing all use in IT becomes a bottleneck.
• A complete ban on generative AI until an…: A blanket ban stops innovation and cannot pre-certify every use.
• No central policy, so each team can decide…: No shared rules leads to inconsistent risk handling.

Key takeaway: Govern AI with shared policies and risk tiers, not bans or a free-for-all.

stem: Employees are pasting confidential customer contracts into a free public chatbot to summarize them. Which response best reduces the risk while meeting the business need?

choices.text: Provide an approved AI tool with data protections for this task and set a clear policy on public tools
Discipline the employees involved and take no further action, since the acceptable-use policy already existed
Allow public chatbots to continue, since summaries do not contain the original contract text
Block all internet access for employees who work with customer contracts until further notice

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Employees turned to public tools because they had a real need. An approved tool with enterprise data protections plus a clear policy addresses both the need and the leakage risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Discipline the employees involved and take…: Punishment alone leaves the need unmet, so the behavior recurs.
• Allow public chatbots to continue, since…: The full contract text is still sent to the public service.
• Block all internet access for employees who…: Blocking internet access is disproportionate and disruptive.

Key takeaway: Meet the business need with approved, protected tools, and set clear usage policies.

stem: A board asks which risk is specific to generative AI compared with traditional predictive models. Which answer is best?

choices.text: Performing worse over time if the business environment changes after the system is deployed
Producing fluent but fabricated content, such as invented citations or facts presented as true
Requiring computing resources and ongoing operating costs to run the system in production
Needing large amounts of historical data to learn patterns before the system can make any useful predictions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Generating convincing but false content (hallucination) is a characteristic risk of generative models. The other items apply to machine learning in general.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Performing worse over time if the business…: Drift affects predictive and generative systems alike.
• Requiring computing resources and ongoing…: All software systems need compute and operating budget.
• Needing large amounts of historical data to…: All machine learning models need training data.

Key takeaway: Hallucination is a hallmark generative AI risk to govern explicitly.

stem: An insurer can choose a slightly more accurate model that cannot explain its decisions or a slightly less accurate model whose reasons are clear. Customers can appeal claim denials. Which choice is most defensible?

choices.text: The more accurate model, because accuracy always outweighs every other consideration in insurance
The more accurate model, with explanations written afterward by staff who guess the model's reasoning
Neither model, because any automated support for claims decisions is inherently irresponsible
The explainable model, because appeals require clear reasons and the accuracy difference is small

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Where people can challenge decisions, the ability to explain them matters. A small accuracy gain rarely justifies losing that ability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The more accurate model, because accuracy…: Accuracy is important but not absolute when decisions affect people.
• The more accurate model, with explanations…: Guessed explanations are not real explanations.
• Neither model, because any automated support…: Well-governed automation with oversight can be responsible.

Key takeaway: When decisions must be explained and appealed, favor explainable models if the accuracy cost is small.

stem: An auditor asks a company for documentation describing each production model's intended use, limitations, training data sources, and evaluation results. Which artifact is designed for this?

choices.text: A model card that records purpose, data, performance, and known limitations for each model
An architecture diagram showing the network paths between the model and the application servers
A cost report listing each model's monthly inference spending and the budget owner responsible
A release note announcing new features to customers each time the model is updated or retrained

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model cards document a model's intended use, data, evaluation results, and limitations, which supports audits and responsible use.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An architecture diagram showing the network…: Diagrams show infrastructure, not model characteristics.
• A cost report listing each model's monthly…: Cost reports track spending, not model behavior.
• A release note announcing new features to…: Release notes communicate changes, not full documentation.

Key takeaway: Model cards are the standard way to document what a model is for and where it falls short.

stem: A bank's customer chatbot must never give investment advice and must hide account numbers in its replies. Which control addresses both requirements consistently?

choices.text: A longer system prompt asking the model politely to avoid advice and account numbers in replies
Training every customer service agent to correct the chatbot when they notice a problem in chats
Guardrails that deny the investment advice topic and mask sensitive information in responses
A weekly manual review of a random sample of conversations to catch violations after they happen

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Configurable guardrails enforce denied topics and sensitive-information filters on every request and response, which is more reliable than instructions alone or after-the-fact review.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A longer system prompt asking the model…: Prompt instructions can be bypassed and are not enforced.
• Training every customer service agent to…: Agents are not present in every chatbot conversation.
• A weekly manual review of a random sample of…: Sampling reviews find problems after customers are affected.

Key takeaway: Enforce content rules with guardrails; prompts and reviews alone are not enough.

stem: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, a company builds a customer chatbot on Amazon Bedrock. Which responsibilities stay with the company? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Maintaining the global network backbone that connects the AWS Regions to each other
Physically securing the data centers where the foundation models are hosted by AWS
Deciding who can access the application and what data is sent in prompts
Patching the underlying servers and hypervisors that run the managed Bedrock service
Configuring guardrails and reviewing how model outputs are used in business decisions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS secures the infrastructure and managed service. The customer controls access, the data it sends, safety configuration, and how outputs are used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Maintaining the global network backbone that…: The global network is operated by AWS.
• Physically securing the data centers where…: Data center security is an AWS responsibility.
• Patching the underlying servers and…: Patching managed service infrastructure is an AWS responsibility.

Key takeaway: With managed AI, AWS secures the service; you own access, data, safeguards, and use of outputs.

stem: A company deploys an AI tool that recommends which employees receive promotions. Which TWO practices best support fairness and accountability? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Keep a human decision-maker responsible for final promotion decisions, with the ability to override
Let the tool make final decisions automatically to remove human bias from the process entirely
Hide the tool's use from managers so they are not influenced by knowing a model was involved
Remove all performance data from the tool so it relies only on tenure when recommending people
Monitor recommendation outcomes across demographic groups and investigate unexplained gaps

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For consequential decisions about people, human accountability and ongoing monitoring of outcomes across groups are central safeguards.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Let the tool make final decisions…: Full automation removes oversight rather than bias.
• Hide the tool's use from managers so they…: Hiding AI use undermines transparency and accountability.
• Remove all performance data from the tool so…: Using only tenure distorts the purpose and can introduce other biases.

Key takeaway: Keep humans accountable and monitor outcomes by group for high-impact decisions about people.

stem: Six months after launch, a fraud model's alerts have become less accurate. Transaction patterns shifted after a new payment method was introduced. Which governance practice would have caught this sooner?

choices.text: A one-time validation of the model before launch, repeated only when the vendor releases a new version of its software
A policy requiring the model to be replaced every month regardless of how well it is performing
An annual report of how many fraud alerts the model generated compared with the previous year
Ongoing monitoring of model performance and input data against agreed thresholds, with alerts to owners

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Models degrade when data or behavior shifts. Continuous monitoring of performance and input distributions with thresholds lets owners detect drift and act early.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A one-time validation of the model before…: One-time validation cannot detect later drift.
• A policy requiring the model to be replaced…: Replacing models on a fixed schedule wastes effort and may not address the cause.
• An annual report of how many fraud alerts…: Annual volume reports are too slow and do not measure accuracy.

Key takeaway: Monitor production models continuously; drift is expected, not exceptional.

stem: A global company is aligning its AI management practices with an international standard so it can show customers a structured, auditable approach. Which standard is designed for an AI management system?

choices.text: PCI DSS, which specifies requirements for protecting payment card data in cardholder environments
ISO/IEC 42001, which specifies requirements for establishing and improving an AI management system
ISO 9001, which specifies requirements for general quality management systems in any industry
ISO/IEC 27017, which gives guidance on information security controls for cloud service providers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ISO/IEC 42001 defines requirements for an AI management system, including governance, risk, and continual improvement for AI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• PCI DSS, which specifies requirements for…: PCI DSS covers payment card data security.
• ISO 9001, which specifies requirements for…: ISO 9001 covers general quality management, not AI specifically.
• ISO/IEC 27017, which gives guidance on…: ISO/IEC 27017 covers cloud security controls.

Key takeaway: ISO/IEC 42001 is the management-system standard for AI.

stem: A retailer's generative AI marketing tool produced an image resembling a competitor's trademarked mascot. Which risk does this illustrate, and which control helps most?

choices.text: Cost risk, reduced by generating fewer images per campaign and reusing older approved assets
Intellectual property risk, reduced by human review of generated assets before publication
Latency risk, reduced by moving the image model to a Region closer to the marketing team
Availability risk, reduced by adding a second image model in case the first becomes unavailable

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Generated content can resemble protected work. Reviewing assets before publication, along with clear usage policies, reduces infringement risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost risk, reduced by generating fewer…: Fewer images does not stop an infringing one from being published.
• Latency risk, reduced by moving the image…: Location affects speed, not IP issues.
• Availability risk, reduced by adding a…: Redundancy does not address content ownership.

Key takeaway: Review generated content for IP issues before it reaches customers.

stem: A company's AI principles state that people affected by an AI decision should be able to get a meaningful reason for it. Which capability supports this principle?

choices.text: Scalability that lets the model handle thousands of additional decisions per second during seasonal demand peaks
Encryption that protects the model's input data while it is stored and while it is in transit
Portability that allows the model to be moved between cloud providers with little rework
Explainability that identifies the main factors behind an individual decision in terms people understand

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Explaining which factors drove a decision, in understandable terms, is what lets affected people receive meaningful reasons.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scalability that lets the model handle…: Scalability concerns capacity.
• Encryption that protects the model's input…: Encryption protects data but does not explain decisions.
• Portability that allows the model to be…: Portability concerns infrastructure flexibility.

Key takeaway: A right to an explanation is delivered through explainability.

stem: A company must prove to auditors that its AI assistant's safety settings were active on every customer conversation last quarter. Which evidence is most convincing?

choices.text: Configuration records for the guardrails plus logs showing they were applied to each invocation
The number of conversations the assistant handled last quarter compared with the quarter before it
An email from the product manager confirming that the team intended to enable the safety settings
A screenshot of the vendor's website describing the safety features that are available for customers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Auditors need evidence of both the control's configuration and its actual use; invocation logs tied to the guardrail show the control was applied.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of conversations the assistant…: Volume says nothing about controls.
• An email from the product manager confirming…: Intent is not evidence of operation.
• A screenshot of the vendor's website…: Available features are not proof they were used.

Key takeaway: Evidence of a control means its configuration plus logs proving it ran.

stem: An airline wants an AI agent that can rebook passengers and issue vouchers automatically. Which TWO controls best limit the risk of costly mistakes? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Disable logging for the agent to protect passenger privacy and keep conversations confidential
Allow the agent to access every airline system so it can solve any problem without escalation
Grant the agent only the specific systems and actions it needs, and log every action taken
Let the agent choose its own voucher amounts based on how upset the passenger seems in chat
Set limits on voucher amounts and require human approval above a threshold

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Limits with human approval for high-value actions and least-privilege access with full logging bound what an agent can do and make its actions reviewable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable logging for the agent to protect…: Without logs, mistakes cannot be detected or audited; privacy is handled by access controls on logs.
• Allow the agent to access every airline…: Broad access widens the impact of errors or manipulation.
• Let the agent choose its own voucher amounts…: Unbounded discretion invites costly and inconsistent outcomes.

Key takeaway: Constrain AI agents with least privilege, spending limits, human approval, and logs.

stem: Before committing to a customer-churn AI project, a telecom company runs a readiness assessment. Which finding is the most serious blocker?

choices.text: Two executives disagree about whether the dashboard should use bar charts or line charts for trends
The company has not yet chosen a name or internal logo for the churn prediction project and its dashboard
Customer records are split across five systems with no shared customer identifier to link them
The marketing team would prefer the project to start in the spring instead of in the winter quarter

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Churn models need a joined view of each customer. Without a common identifier, data cannot be combined reliably, which blocks the project until it is fixed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Two executives disagree about whether the…: Chart style is a presentation detail.
• The company has not yet chosen a name or…: Naming has no effect on feasibility.
• The marketing team would prefer the project…: Timing preferences are easy to resolve.

Key takeaway: Data that cannot be joined or trusted is the most common AI readiness blocker.

stem: An executive asks how an AI maturity assessment differs from a capability gap analysis. Which answer is accurate?

choices.text: A maturity assessment measures model accuracy, while a gap analysis measures how much the AI budget has been spent so far
They are identical activities with different names, used interchangeably by consultants and technology vendors
A maturity assessment is required by law in every country, while a gap analysis is an optional internal exercise
A maturity assessment places the organization on stages of AI capability; a gap analysis lists what is missing for a specific goal

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Maturity models describe where an organization stands overall across stages; gap analysis identifies the specific skills, data, or processes needed for a defined objective.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A maturity assessment measures model…: Neither measures model accuracy or spending.
• They are identical activities with different…: They answer different questions.
• A maturity assessment is required by law in…: Neither is universally required by law.

Key takeaway: Maturity shows where you are overall; gap analysis shows what you need for a specific goal.

stem: A manufacturer's AI demand forecasts are unreliable because each plant records inventory differently. Which foundational investment helps most?

choices.text: A more powerful foundation model that can guess what each plant's inventory records actually mean
Common data definitions and a shared, governed data platform that all plants feed consistently
More dashboards so each plant manager can view the unreliable forecasts in more places at once
A new AI vendor, since unreliable forecasts show that the current vendor's algorithms are weak

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Consistent definitions and a governed data platform give models reliable inputs; no algorithm can fully fix inconsistent source data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A more powerful foundation model that can…: Guessing meaning adds error rather than removing it.
• More dashboards so each plant manager can…: More views of bad forecasts do not improve them.
• A new AI vendor, since unreliable forecasts…: The issue is data consistency, not the vendor.

Key takeaway: Fix data foundations before expecting reliable AI outputs.

stem: Employees fear an AI assistant will replace their jobs, and adoption is low three months after launch. Which leadership action is most effective?

choices.text: Explain how the assistant supports their roles, involve them in improving it, and offer role-specific training
Require every employee to use the assistant daily and publish a ranking of the lowest users each week
Replace the current assistant with a different product, since low adoption proves the tool is inadequate
Stop communicating about the assistant so employees gradually forget about their concerns over time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Adoption problems rooted in fear respond to clear purpose, involvement, and skills building. Mandates and silence tend to deepen resistance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Require every employee to use the assistant…: Coercion and public rankings increase fear and resentment.
• Replace the current assistant with a…: The cause is concern about jobs, not the product.
• Stop communicating about the assistant so…: Silence leaves fears unaddressed.

Key takeaway: Address fear with purpose, involvement, and training; mandates rarely build real adoption.

stem: A generative AI pilot succeeded in one department. Leadership wants company-wide rollout within a year. Which approach best manages risk?

choices.text: Deploy to every department on the same day so all employees benefit from the tool at the same time
Expand in phases to a few more departments, measure results, and refine before a broad rollout
Keep the tool in the pilot department permanently, since success elsewhere cannot be guaranteed
Rebuild the solution from scratch for each department so that every team gets a fully custom tool

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Phased expansion tests whether results hold in different contexts and lets the team fix problems while the blast radius is small.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deploy to every department on the same day…: A big-bang rollout multiplies the impact of any problem.
• Keep the tool in the pilot department…: Refusing to scale forfeits proven value.
• Rebuild the solution from scratch for each…: Rebuilding for every team wastes effort and slows adoption.

Key takeaway: Scale AI in phases, with measurement and refinement between waves.

stem: An AI proof of concept performed well in testing but failed within weeks of going into production because nobody monitored it or planned for outages. What was missing?

choices.text: Production practices such as monitoring, versioning, rollback, and a continuity plan for failures
A more expensive foundation model, since cheaper models are the main reason production systems fail
A formal launch event, since systems launched without executive attention are more likely to fail
A larger test dataset, since proofs of concept that pass testing never fail once they reach production

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Moving from experiment to production requires operational practices: monitoring, controlled releases, rollback, and a plan for when the system fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A more expensive foundation model, since…: Model price is not the root cause described.
• A formal launch event, since systems…: Launch events do not keep systems running.
• A larger test dataset, since proofs of…: Passing tests does not guarantee production success.

Key takeaway: Production AI needs operations: monitoring, rollback, and continuity planning.

stem: A company wants AI skills across the business quickly on a limited budget, and also needs buy-in from teams. Which workforce approach fits best?

choices.text: Replace the existing workforce with newly hired AI specialists over the next two quarters
Wait until universities produce enough AI graduates before starting any internal AI projects
Outsource all AI work permanently so that no employee needs to learn anything about AI
Upskill motivated employees who know the business, and add a few specialist hires for hard gaps

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Upskilling people with domain knowledge builds capability and buy-in at lower cost, while targeted hires fill gaps that training cannot cover quickly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replace the existing workforce with newly…: Mass replacement is costly and destroys institutional knowledge and trust.
• Wait until universities produce enough AI…: Waiting delays value indefinitely.
• Outsource all AI work permanently so that no…: Permanent outsourcing leaves the business unable to judge or direct AI.

Key takeaway: Upskill domain experts and hire selectively to build AI capability with buy-in.

stem: A company's on-premises data center cannot handle unpredictable spikes in AI inference demand, and buying hardware for peak load would sit idle most of the year. Which option best addresses this?

choices.text: Reject inference requests during demand spikes so the existing on-premises hardware is never overloaded
Limit the AI system to a fixed number of users so that demand never exceeds on-premises capacity limits
Move suitable inference workloads to cloud services that scale with demand and are billed by use
Buy enough on-premises GPUs for peak demand and accept that most of them will sit idle most of the year

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Elastic cloud capacity matches unpredictable demand without paying for idle peak hardware.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reject inference requests during demand…: Rejecting requests harms users and value.
• Limit the AI system to a fixed number of…: Capping users limits value to protect infrastructure.
• Buy enough on-premises GPUs for peak demand…: Buying for peak locks capital into idle equipment.

Key takeaway: Use elastic, pay-per-use capacity when AI demand is spiky.

stem: A company is moving a generative AI assistant from pilot to use by 5,000 employees. Which TWO preparations are most important? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Replacing the pilot's approved model with the newest model released that same week
A business continuity plan for how work continues if the assistant is unavailable
Removing the feedback button so employees are not distracted from their daily work tasks
A new internal logo and brand name for the assistant before the wider rollout begins
Monitoring, logging, and rollback procedures for the production system

explanation:
Why this is correct:
At scale, the organization needs to detect and recover from problems, and to keep operating when the assistant is down.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replacing the pilot's approved model with…: Switching to an untested model right before rollout adds risk.
• Removing the feedback button so employees…: Feedback is essential for improvement at scale.
• A new internal logo and brand name for the…: Branding does not affect production readiness.

Key takeaway: Production readiness means observability, rollback, and continuity planning.

stem: After deploying AI that classifies incoming support tickets, a company redefines agents' roles. Which change reflects a healthy human-AI operating model?

choices.text: Agents move from manual sorting to handling exceptions, complex cases, and reviewing AI decisions
Agents are removed from the process entirely, and customers are told to email the AI system directly
Agents continue sorting every ticket by hand while the AI system classifies the same tickets in parallel
Agents are asked to hide misclassifications so the AI system's reported accuracy stays high for leadership

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AI takes over repetitive classification, and people focus on judgment-heavy work and oversight, which improves both efficiency and quality.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Agents are removed from the process…: Removing people eliminates oversight and exception handling.
• Agents continue sorting every ticket by hand…: Duplicating work wastes the benefit.
• Agents are asked to hide misclassifications…: Hiding errors undermines improvement and trust.

Key takeaway: Redesign roles so people handle judgment and oversight while AI handles routine work.

stem: A healthcare company wants to use generative AI on patient records. Which readiness element must be in place before any use case proceeds?

choices.text: A plan for which department will present the AI results at the next all-hands company meeting
A decision on whether the AI assistant's interface will use a light theme or a dark theme
Data governance covering consent, access controls, and privacy obligations for the records
A list of competitors that have already announced generative AI projects in healthcare markets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sensitive data requires governance for consent, access, and privacy before it can be used responsibly and lawfully.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A plan for which department will present the…: Presentation plans do not affect readiness.
• A decision on whether the AI assistant's…: Interface themes are cosmetic.
• A list of competitors that have already…: Competitor lists do not address data obligations.

Key takeaway: With sensitive data, governance comes before use cases.

stem: An AI readiness assessment finds strong executive enthusiasm but staff who lack skills and are anxious about change. Which TWO actions address the readiness gap? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Limit AI discussions to executives until all tools have been fully deployed company-wide
Accelerate the rollout so that staff have no time to worry before the tools arrive
Buy more AI tools, since having more options will increase staff confidence on its own
Run role-based training that shows staff how AI applies to their own work
Set up a change-management plan with clear communication and channels for feedback

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The gap is people readiness. Relevant training builds skills, and structured change management addresses anxiety through communication and involvement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Limit AI discussions to executives until all…: Excluding staff from discussions deepens the gap.
• Accelerate the rollout so that staff have no…: Rushing increases anxiety and resistance.
• Buy more AI tools, since having more options…: More tools do not create skills or reduce anxiety.

Key takeaway: Close people readiness gaps with training and change management.

stem: A company has three AI pilots running. One exceeds targets, one is on track, and one has missed milestones twice with no clear fix. How should leadership manage the portfolio?

choices.text: Continue all three pilots equally, since stopping any of them would signal failure to the organization
Scale the successful pilot, continue the on-track one, and stop the one that keeps missing milestones
Move budget from the successful pilot to the failing one, since the failing pilot needs the most help
Stop all three pilots and restart with new ideas, since mixed results show the strategy is unclear

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Portfolio discipline means investing more in what works, continuing what is progressing, and stopping initiatives that repeatedly miss milestones without a path forward.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Continue all three pilots equally, since…: Equal treatment ignores evidence.
• Move budget from the successful pilot to the…: Starving the winner to rescue a failing pilot misallocates resources.
• Stop all three pilots and restart with new…: Stopping successes wastes proven value.

Key takeaway: Scale winners, stop repeated misses, and let evidence drive AI portfolio decisions.

stem: A company names an 'AI champion' in each department. What is the main purpose of this role in an AI transformation?

choices.text: Approve every AI-related purchase in the department without involving finance or procurement
Build all of the department's AI models personally so that no other employee has to learn AI
Help peers adopt AI in their daily work, gather feedback, and share practical lessons across teams
Monitor colleagues and report anyone who has not yet used the company's approved AI tools

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Champions spread practical know-how, surface feedback, and connect teams, which accelerates adoption from within.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Approve every AI-related purchase in the…: Purchasing authority is a governance role, not the champion role.
• Build all of the department's AI models…: Champions support others; they do not do all the work.
• Monitor colleagues and report anyone who has…: Surveillance undermines trust and adoption.

Key takeaway: AI champions drive peer adoption and feedback loops.

stem: A retailer wants several AI use cases next year but each team currently builds its own data pipelines. Which foundational investment best supports scaling?

choices.text: A freeze on all data engineering work until the AI use cases are fully defined and approved
A separate data warehouse for each new AI use case so that no team depends on any other team
A policy that every AI project must collect brand-new data rather than reusing existing data
A shared, governed data platform with reusable pipelines and a common catalog of trusted datasets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shared, governed data foundations let new use cases reuse trusted data instead of rebuilding pipelines, which speeds delivery and improves consistency.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A freeze on all data engineering work until…: Freezing data work delays every use case.
• A separate data warehouse for each new AI…: Separate warehouses multiply cost and inconsistency.
• A policy that every AI project must collect…: Refusing to reuse data wastes existing assets.

Key takeaway: Reusable, governed data foundations are what let AI scale beyond one project.

stem: A COO asks how machine learning differs from traditional software for automating loan pre-screening. Which explanation is most accurate?

choices.text: Machine learning learns decision patterns from historical examples, while traditional software follows rules that people write explicitly
Machine learning needs no data to operate once installed, while traditional software needs large datasets before it can make decisions
Machine learning always produces exact, repeatable answers, while traditional software makes probabilistic guesses about each applicant
Machine learning can only run on premises, while traditional software can only run on cloud infrastructure in regulated industries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Traditional programs apply explicit rules; machine learning infers patterns from examples, which suits problems where rules are hard to write down.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Machine learning needs no data to operate…: ML depends on data to learn.
• Machine learning always produces exact,…: It is the reverse: rule-based code is deterministic, and ML outputs are probabilistic.
• Machine learning can only run on premises,…: Both run in either environment.

Key takeaway: Rules are written for traditional software; patterns are learned by machine learning.

stem: A retailer's model predicts which customers will buy winter coats. Leaders ask what a 'feature' is when the data team says 'last season's purchases is our strongest feature.' Which explanation is right?

choices.text: A feature is an input variable the model uses to make predictions, such as a customer's past purchases
A feature is the final prediction the model produces for each customer, such as buy or not buy
A feature is the algorithm that was selected for the project, such as a decision tree or a neural network
A feature is a new capability added to the retailer's website, such as a wish list or a gift card option

explanation:
Why this is correct:
In machine learning, features are the input variables describing each example; the model learns how they relate to the outcome.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A feature is the final prediction the model…: The prediction is the output or label, not a feature.
• A feature is the algorithm that was selected…: The algorithm is the method, not an input.
• A feature is a new capability added to the…: That is a product feature, not a model input.

Key takeaway: Features are the inputs; the label or prediction is the output.

stem: A bank wants to spot unusual card transactions that do not match any known fraud pattern, because fraudsters keep changing tactics. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Rules that block only transactions matching fraud patterns seen in last year's confirmed cases
Anomaly detection that learns normal behavior and flags transactions that deviate from it
A translation model that converts transaction data into several languages for global review
A text generation model that writes a description of each transaction for analysts to read

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When new fraud types appear, learning what normal looks like and flagging deviations catches cases that known-pattern rules miss.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rules that block only transactions matching…: Known-pattern rules miss new tactics.
• A translation model that converts…: Translation does not identify unusual behavior.
• A text generation model that writes a…: Descriptions do not detect anything.

Key takeaway: Use anomaly detection when the threat keeps changing and labeled examples lag behind.

stem: A media company wants to automatically add captions to thousands of recorded interviews. Which AI capability is the core requirement?

choices.text: Text-to-speech that converts written captions into spoken narration for each interview
Sentiment analysis that scores whether each interviewee sounded positive or negative overall
Speech-to-text transcription that converts spoken words in audio into written text
Image classification that labels the objects that appear in each video frame of the interviews

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Captions require converting speech to text; services such as Amazon Transcribe do this at scale.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Text-to-speech that converts written…: That is the reverse direction.
• Sentiment analysis that scores whether each…: Tone scores do not produce captions.
• Image classification that labels the objects…: Object labels are not captions of speech.

Key takeaway: Captions start with speech-to-text.

stem: A product owner sees a model with a '200,000-token context window' in a proposal. What does this mean for the business?

choices.text: The model can serve 200,000 users at the same time without slowing down or queuing any requests
The model will cost 200,000 dollars per month regardless of how much it is actually used
The model has been trained on exactly 200,000 documents, which limits how much it knows about the world
The model can consider roughly that much text at once, such as a long document plus a question

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The context window is how much input and conversation the model can take into account in one request; larger windows allow longer documents in a single prompt.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The model can serve 200,000 users at the…: Concurrency depends on service capacity, not the context window.
• The model will cost 200,000 dollars per…: Pricing is usually per token used, not a fixed amount.
• The model has been trained on exactly…: Training data size is unrelated to the context window.

Key takeaway: Context window = how much text the model can consider in one request.

stem: A company wants its assistant to answer only from approved HR policies and to say 'I don't know' otherwise. Which combination best achieves this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Raise the temperature so the model explores more possible answers before replying
Retrieve relevant policy passages and instruct the model to answer only from them
Fine-tune the model on public internet forums so it learns how employees ask questions
Remove the policy documents so the model relies entirely on its general training data
Apply a grounding check that blocks answers not supported by the retrieved passages

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Retrieval supplies the approved content, and a grounding check filters answers not supported by it, which together keep answers within approved sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Raise the temperature so the model explores…: Higher temperature increases variety and the chance of unsupported content.
• Fine-tune the model on public internet…: Forum text does not teach the company's policies.
• Remove the policy documents so the model…: General training data is not the approved policy.

Key takeaway: Ground answers in approved content and verify that the answer is supported by it.

stem: A logistics firm's model predicts delivery delays with 90% accuracy, but 95% of deliveries are on time. Why should leadership be cautious about the 90% figure?

choices.text: A model that always predicts 'on time' would score 95%, so accuracy alone hides how well delays are caught
Accuracy above 85% is always suspicious and usually means the model was trained on test data
Delivery data changes daily, so any accuracy figure becomes meaningless within the first 24 hours after training
90% accuracy guarantees that 90% of late deliveries will be detected before customers complain

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With imbalanced outcomes, accuracy can look good while the model misses most of the rare but important cases. Recall and precision on delays tell the real story.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy above 85% is always suspicious and…: High accuracy is not inherently suspicious.
• Delivery data changes daily, so any accuracy…: Performance can drift, but it does not vanish daily.
• 90% accuracy guarantees that 90% of late…: Accuracy is not recall on the late class.

Key takeaway: With rare events, judge models on how well they catch those events, not on overall accuracy.

stem: A travel company wants an assistant that answers questions about its own booking policies. It has no labeled training data but has well-written policy documents. Which approach fits best at the start?

choices.text: Collect and label 100,000 example questions before any development can begin on the assistant
Build a rules engine with one hand-written rule for every question a customer might possibly ask
Train a new language model from scratch on the policy documents so it understands the company
Use a foundation model with retrieval over the policy documents, without training a new model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A pre-trained foundation model plus retrieval over existing documents delivers useful answers quickly without labeled data or custom training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Collect and label 100,000 example questions…: Large labeling efforts are unnecessary for this use case.
• Build a rules engine with one hand-written…: Rules for every possible question do not scale.
• Train a new language model from scratch on…: Training a language model from scratch is costly and unneeded.

Key takeaway: Start with foundation models and retrieval when you have good documents but no labeled data.

stem: A marketing team gets generic output when it asks a model to 'write an email about our sale.' Which prompt change would most improve relevance?

choices.text: Repeat the same short request several times in a row so the model understands that this particular task is very important
Remove all details from the prompt so the model has complete creative freedom to decide the content
Specify the audience, the offer details, the tone, the length, and include an example of a past successful email
Ask the model to write the email in capital letters so the output stands out more to the recipient

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clear context, constraints, and examples guide the model toward relevant, on-brand output. This is prompt engineering, and it requires no retraining.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Repeat the same short request several times…: Repetition does not add information.
• Remove all details from the prompt so the…: Less context usually makes output more generic.
• Ask the model to write the email in capital…: Formatting does not add relevance.

Key takeaway: Better prompts supply context, constraints, and examples.

stem: A leadership team is choosing how to adapt a foundation model. Which statement correctly compares prompt engineering and fine-tuning?

choices.text: Prompt engineering and fine-tuning are the same technique, described differently by different vendors
Prompt engineering changes the input and is fast to iterate; fine-tuning changes model weights and needs data and training
Prompt engineering requires thousands of labeled examples; fine-tuning works without any training data at all
Prompt engineering permanently retrains the model; fine-tuning only changes the wording of each request

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Prompt engineering shapes behavior through the input, so it is quick and cheap to change; fine-tuning adjusts the model with training data, which costs more but can embed consistent behavior.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prompt engineering and fine-tuning are the…: They are distinct techniques.
• Prompt engineering requires thousands of…: Fine-tuning needs data; prompting does not.
• Prompt engineering permanently retrains the…: The descriptions are reversed.

Key takeaway: Try prompting first; fine-tune when you need consistent behavior that prompts cannot achieve.

stem: A company must choose between a classification model and a generative model for routing emails to five departments. Which reasoning is sound?

choices.text: Generative models are always better because they are newer and can write longer, more detailed answers
Generative models are required whenever the input contains more than one sentence of natural language
Classification fits because the output is one of a fixed set of labels and can be measured precisely
Classification cannot handle text, so only a generative model can read the content of incoming emails

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Routing to a fixed set of categories is a classification task; its outputs are easy to measure and control. A generative model is not required.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Generative models are always better because…: Newer is not automatically better for a labeling task.
• Generative models are required whenever the…: Sentence count does not dictate the approach.
• Classification cannot handle text, so only a…: Text classification is a mature technique.

Key takeaway: When the answer is one of a fixed set, classification is usually the simpler, more controllable fit.

stem: A hospital asks why its image model needs thousands of labeled X-rays when a general foundation model 'already knows about medicine.' Which explanation is best?

choices.text: Task-specific labeled examples teach the model the exact patterns and categories this diagnostic task requires
Foundation models cannot process any kind of image, so labeled X-rays are needed to teach them what pixels and images are
Labeled data is only a legal formality and does not affect the model's performance on real patients
General foundation models are never used in healthcare, so the hospital must always train from scratch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
General knowledge does not guarantee reliable performance on a narrow clinical task. Labeled examples define the categories and teach the specific visual patterns the task needs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Foundation models cannot process any kind of…: Many foundation models handle images.
• Labeled data is only a legal formality and…: Labels directly shape what the model learns.
• General foundation models are never used in…: Foundation models are adapted for healthcare uses.

Key takeaway: Specialized, high-stakes tasks need task-specific labeled data even when starting from a foundation model.

stem: A company's assistant must answer questions about data in a large internal database, such as 'total sales by region last quarter.' Which approach is most reliable?

choices.text: Fine-tune the model weekly on the database so it memorizes every sales figure for each region
Paste the entire database into every prompt so the model can read all of the rows at once
Ask the model to estimate the sales totals from its general training data and present them as facts
Have the model generate a database query, run it against the database, and summarize the actual results

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Numbers should come from the database itself. Generating a query and running it keeps answers exact and current, with the model handling the language.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fine-tune the model weekly on the database…: Memorizing changing numbers through retraining is slow and unreliable.
• Paste the entire database into every prompt…: Entire databases do not fit in prompts and would be costly.
• Ask the model to estimate the sales totals…: The model cannot know internal figures and would invent them.

Key takeaway: For exact figures, let the model query the data rather than recall it.

stem: A retailer wants to forecast store staffing needs for each hour of next month. Which TWO data characteristics matter most for this forecasting problem? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Employee preferences for music played in the store, recorded in the latest staff satisfaction survey
The brand of point-of-sale terminal each store uses, since terminal brand predicts future traffic
Historical hourly foot traffic and sales with enough seasons to capture weekly and holiday patterns
The color and style of each store's signage, since signage design determines hourly staffing needs
Known upcoming events such as promotions and holidays that will change expected demand

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Time-series forecasting relies on historical patterns over enough periods and on known future events that shift demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Employee preferences for music played in the…: Music preferences are unrelated to traffic.
• The brand of point-of-sale terminal each…: Terminal brand does not predict visits.
• The color and style of each store's signage,…: Signage design does not drive hourly demand.

Key takeaway: Forecasts need rich history and known future drivers.

stem: A utility company's leadership wants AI to support its goal of cutting unplanned outages by 20% in two years. Which initiative aligns most directly with that goal?

choices.text: Predictive maintenance that flags equipment likely to fail so crews can fix it before an outage
A chatbot that answers billing questions so the call center can reduce average wait times on the phone
A generative AI tool that writes the company's quarterly newsletter for residential customers each month
An image generator that produces marketing visuals for the company's renewable energy advertising campaigns

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Strategy alignment means choosing initiatives that move the stated goal. Predicting equipment failures directly reduces unplanned outages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A chatbot that answers billing questions so…: Billing support may be valuable but does not reduce outages.
• A generative AI tool that writes the…: Newsletters do not affect outages.
• An image generator that produces marketing…: Marketing visuals do not affect reliability.

Key takeaway: Link each AI initiative to a specific business goal it can measurably move.

stem: A company can fund either an AI initiative with modest, fairly certain savings or one with large but uncertain upside. It has little AI experience. Which approach is most sensible?

choices.text: Split the budget evenly and run both at full scale immediately, regardless of the organization's experience level
Fund only the large uncertain initiative, since the biggest possible upside should always be pursued first
Fund neither until both initiatives can be guaranteed to succeed, since any failure would harm the company's reputation with investors
Fund the more certain initiative first to build capability and credibility, and plan a staged test of the larger bet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With limited experience, a surer win builds skills, trust, and evidence, while a staged test of the bigger idea keeps its upside open with less risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Split the budget evenly and run both at full…: Running both at scale ignores capability limits.
• Fund only the large uncertain initiative,…: All-in on uncertain upside is high risk for an inexperienced team.
• Fund neither until both initiatives can be…: No initiative can be guaranteed.

Key takeaway: Build capability with surer wins and test big bets in stages.

stem: A company deployed an AI tool to speed up contract review. After six months, review time fell 30%, but two costly clauses slipped through. How should value be assessed?

choices.text: Ignore the missed clauses, since human reviewers also miss clauses and some errors are therefore unavoidable in any process
Weigh the time savings against the cost of the missed clauses and adjust review controls to protect quality
Report only the 30% time reduction, since efficiency is the only metric that executives care about
Stop using the tool immediately, since any error at all proves that AI cannot be used for legal work

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Net value includes both gains and the cost of new errors. Measuring both and adjusting controls, such as human review of high-risk clauses, protects the gain.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ignore the missed clauses, since human…: Unmanaged errors erode value and trust.
• Report only the 30% time reduction, since…: Ignoring quality overstates value.
• Stop using the tool immediately, since any…: One failure mode can often be controlled rather than abandoning the benefit.

Key takeaway: Net value = gains minus the cost of new errors; manage both.

stem: A CFO asks what 'total cost of ownership' should include for a generative AI assistant. Which list is most complete?

choices.text: Only the vendor license fee, since internal staff time is already paid for through the existing salaries of the team
Model usage, integration and development, data preparation, monitoring and support, and staff training
Only the per-token model charges shown on the monthly cloud bill for the production environment
Only the one-time development cost, since ongoing running costs are covered by the savings produced

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TCO covers everything required to build, run, and sustain the solution, including people, data, integration, and operations, not just model charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only the vendor license fee, since internal…: Staff time spent on the solution is a real cost.
• Only the per-token model charges shown on…: Usage fees are only one component.
• Only the one-time development cost, since…: Ongoing costs must be counted separately from savings.

Key takeaway: TCO includes build, run, data, people, and support costs.

stem: An AI project will cost $300,000 per year and is expected to save $450,000 per year starting in year two, after a $200,000 setup cost in year one with no savings. Which statement about payback is correct?

choices.text: Year one costs $500,000 with no savings; from year two it nets $150,000 a year, so payback takes over four years in total
The project pays back in year one, since the $450,000 savings exceed the $300,000 annual cost
The project never pays back, since annual costs are higher than the setup cost in every year of the project
The project pays back in exactly two years, since setup and running costs are recovered by the first savings

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Year one spends $500,000 ($200,000 setup plus $300,000 running) with no savings. From year two the net gain is $150,000 a year, so recovering $500,000 takes about 3.3 years after year one, over four years in total.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The project pays back in year one, since the…: No savings arrive in year one.
• The project never pays back, since annual…: Net annual savings of $150,000 eventually recover the investment.
• The project pays back in exactly two years,…: $150,000 a year does not recover $500,000 in one year.

Key takeaway: Include setup costs and delayed benefits when computing payback.

stem: A specialty insurer wants to differentiate with AI. Competitors can license the same underwriting AI products. Which strategy creates the most defensible advantage?

choices.text: License the same underwriting product as competitors, but deploy it faster than any of them manage to
Reduce prices across all products and rely on AI-driven efficiency to make up the lost margin later
Publicize the AI initiative widely, since market perception of innovation is itself a durable competitive advantage
Combine AI with its proprietary loss data and expert underwriting workflows to price niche risks better

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Advantage lasts when it rests on assets competitors cannot copy, such as proprietary data and expert processes, applied to a specific area where they matter.

Why the other options are wrong:
• License the same underwriting product as…: Speed with an identical product is a temporary edge.
• Reduce prices across all products and rely…: Price cuts are easily matched and erode margins.
• Publicize the AI initiative widely, since…: Perception without substance fades.

Key takeaway: Defensible AI advantage comes from proprietary data and expertise, not access to common tools.

stem: A company is deciding whether to build or buy an AI solution for internal expense auditing. The process is standard across industries and not a differentiator. Which option usually fits?

choices.text: Build a custom solution from scratch, since owning the code is always more valuable than buying
Delay the decision until the company can build a custom foundation model for all internal processes
Buy or use a managed solution, and invest internal effort where the company differentiates
Build a solution only if the vendor refuses to provide a discount of at least half the list price

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For standard, non-differentiating processes, buying or using managed services is typically faster and cheaper, freeing internal capacity for differentiating work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Build a custom solution from scratch, since…: Owning code has costs and rarely pays off for commodity processes.
• Delay the decision until the company can…: A custom foundation model is unnecessary here.
• Build a solution only if the vendor refuses…: Discounts do not change the strategic logic.

Key takeaway: Buy for commodity processes; build where you differentiate.

stem: A hotel chain's AI strategy lists 'use generative AI everywhere' as its top objective. What is the main weakness of this objective?

choices.text: It excludes predictive AI, which is the only type of AI that can deliver value for hospitality businesses
It names a technology rather than a business outcome, so success cannot be measured or prioritized
It is too specific, since strategies should avoid mentioning any technology or measurable target at all
It is too narrow, since the hotel chain should also commit to using quantum computing everywhere

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Objectives should describe outcomes, such as guest satisfaction or revenue per room, that AI helps achieve. Technology-centric goals cannot guide prioritization or measurement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• It excludes predictive AI, which is the only…: Generative AI can create value in hospitality too.
• It is too specific, since strategies should…: Good strategies include measurable targets.
• It is too narrow, since the hotel chain…: Adding technologies worsens the problem.

Key takeaway: State AI objectives as business outcomes, not technology adoption.

stem: A company launched an AI assistant for employees. Which leading indicator best signals whether it will eventually deliver business value?

choices.text: Repeat usage on the intended tasks, together with user-reported time saved on those tasks
The number of employees who opened the assistant once during the first week after its launch
The total number of tokens processed by the assistant since launch across every department
The number of press articles that mentioned the company's assistant during the launch month

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sustained use on target tasks, plus early evidence of time saved, indicates the tool is embedded in work, which precedes measurable outcomes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of employees who opened the…: One-time trials show curiosity, not value.
• The total number of tokens processed by the…: Token volume measures cost, not usefulness.
• The number of press articles that mentioned…: Press coverage is not adoption or value.

Key takeaway: Track sustained, task-relevant usage as a leading indicator of value.

stem: A company considers training its own large language model to reduce dependence on providers. Which consideration most often argues against this?

choices.text: Existing foundation models cannot be customized in any way, so training a new model from scratch is the only real option
Custom models cannot be deployed on AWS and must always run in the company's own data centers
Custom-trained models are legally prohibited from using any of the company's internal documents
The cost, data, and expertise required are very large compared with adapting existing foundation models

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Training a large model requires massive compute, data, and specialized talent. Most companies get better returns from adapting existing models with prompting, retrieval, or fine-tuning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Existing foundation models cannot be…: Foundation models can be customized in several ways.
• Custom models cannot be deployed on AWS and…: Custom models can be deployed on AWS.
• Custom-trained models are legally prohibited…: No such blanket prohibition exists.

Key takeaway: Adapting existing models usually beats training your own from scratch.

stem: A company's AI roadmap should connect initiatives to strategy. Which TWO elements belong in each initiative's definition? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The names of every vendor the company has ever contacted about artificial intelligence
The specific GPU instance type the engineers expect to use during development
The business outcome it targets and how success will be measured
The fonts and color palette that will be used for the initiative's status dashboard
The key dependencies, such as data, skills, and systems needed to deliver it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Outcomes and measures show why the initiative matters, and dependencies show what it takes to deliver, which together make the roadmap plannable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The names of every vendor the company has…: Vendor history is not part of an initiative definition.
• The specific GPU instance type the engineers…: Instance types are engineering details decided later.
• The fonts and color palette that will be…: Dashboard styling is cosmetic.

Key takeaway: Define initiatives by outcome, measure, and dependencies.

stem: A company must decide whether to expand an AI pilot. Which TWO measures best show whether scaling will create value? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The number of features the pilot team added to the tool during the most recent sprint cycle
The model's benchmark score on a public leaderboard compared with other available models
The number of internal presentations the pilot team gave about the project to other departments and leaders
Measured improvement in the target business metric compared with a baseline or control group
The projected cost to operate at full scale, including support, monitoring, and change management

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scaling decisions need evidence of real impact and a realistic view of full-scale costs. Together they show whether benefits will exceed costs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of features the pilot team added…: Feature counts measure activity.
• The model's benchmark score on a public…: Public benchmarks do not show value in this business.
• The number of internal presentations the…: Presentations measure visibility, not value.

Key takeaway: Scale on measured impact versus full operating cost.

stem: A retailer wants to use AI to improve its competitive position but fears it lacks talent. Which approach best balances speed and building lasting capability?

choices.text: Copy a competitor's announced AI features exactly, since imitation avoids the need for any expertise
Pause all AI plans for three years until the retailer can hire a complete in-house research organization
Partner with an experienced provider for the first project while training an internal team to take over
Outsource all AI work permanently so that the retailer never needs to understand how its AI systems work

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Partnering delivers early results while knowledge transfer builds internal capability, reducing long-term dependence.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copy a competitor's announced AI features…: Imitation does not create lasting advantage or capability.
• Pause all AI plans for three years until the…: A long pause cedes ground to competitors.
• Outsource all AI work permanently so that…: Permanent outsourcing leaves the retailer unable to guide or evaluate its AI.

Key takeaway: Partner to start fast, and build internal capability through knowledge transfer.

stem: An AI demand-forecasting tool improved forecast accuracy, but inventory costs did not fall. Which explanation is most likely?

choices.text: The model is too accurate, and highly accurate forecasts always increase inventory holding costs
Planners kept ordering the same way instead of acting on the better forecasts
Inventory costs are only affected by warehouse rent, so forecasting tools are irrelevant to them
Forecast accuracy never affects inventory costs, so the improvement was never going to matter

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Value depends on decisions changing. If ordering processes did not adopt the forecasts, better predictions cannot reduce inventory.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The model is too accurate, and highly…: Accuracy does not raise costs by itself.
• Inventory costs are only affected by…: Inventory costs depend heavily on how much is ordered.
• Forecast accuracy never affects inventory…: Better forecasts can reduce excess and shortage costs when acted on.

Key takeaway: AI creates value only when decisions and processes change to use it.

stem: A company has an AI use case with high value but depends on data it does not yet collect. Another has moderate value and data ready today. How should sequencing work?

choices.text: Start the ready use case now, and begin collecting the needed data so the higher-value case can follow
Wait to start either use case until the missing data has been collected for at least five years
Cancel the high-value use case, since use cases requiring new data collection should never be pursued
Start the high-value use case immediately and let the model learn without any of the required data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sequencing by readiness delivers value now while preparing the data foundation for the larger opportunity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Wait to start either use case until the…: Waiting years forfeits the value available now.
• Cancel the high-value use case, since use…: New data collection is often worthwhile for high value.
• Start the high-value use case immediately…: A model cannot learn from data that does not exist.

Key takeaway: Sequence AI work by readiness while investing in data for bigger opportunities.

stem: A bank is negotiating with an AI vendor. Which TWO contract terms best protect the bank's long-term position? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Restrictions on the vendor using the bank's data to train models offered to others
A commitment that the bank will use the vendor exclusively for every future AI project
A promise that the vendor will attend the bank's quarterly executive meetings in person
A clause allowing the vendor to change pricing at any time without prior notice to the bank
Clear rights to export its data and configurations if it ends the relationship

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data portability limits lock-in, and restrictions on reusing the bank's data protect its confidentiality and competitive advantage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A commitment that the bank will use the…: Exclusivity increases lock-in.
• A promise that the vendor will attend the…: Meeting attendance does not protect the bank's interests.
• A clause allowing the vendor to change…: Unilateral price changes weaken the bank's position.

Key takeaway: Protect data rights and portability in AI contracts.

stem: Two AI initiatives both claim $1 million in annual value. One reduces costs in a process that is already measured precisely; the other claims 'improved brand perception.' How should a steering committee treat these claims?

choices.text: Reject both initiatives, since no AI benefit can ever be measured with enough precision to fund it
Treat both claims as equally certain, since both teams estimated the same annual dollar value for the committee
Give more weight to the measurable cost reduction and ask the brand initiative for a way to measure its impact
Give more weight to the brand initiative, since intangible benefits always exceed measurable cost savings

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Claims backed by precise measurement are more reliable. Intangible benefits can be real but need a measurement approach before they carry equal weight.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reject both initiatives, since no AI benefit…: Many AI benefits are measurable.
• Treat both claims as equally certain, since…: Equal estimates do not mean equal certainty.
• Give more weight to the brand initiative,…: Intangible benefits are not automatically larger.

Key takeaway: Weight AI value claims by how well they can be measured.

stem: A company's executives each champion different AI ideas, and projects stall in debate. What would most improve decision-making?
