choices.text: Choose ideas by random draw to remove politics from the decision entirely and move faster
Agree on shared evaluation criteria tied to strategy and apply them consistently to every proposal
Let the executive with the largest budget decide which AI ideas proceed each quarter without review
Approve every executive's favorite idea so that nobody feels overruled during the planning process

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shared, strategy-linked criteria make trade-offs transparent and depersonalize decisions, which unblocks prioritization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Choose ideas by random draw to remove…: Random choice ignores value and feasibility.
• Let the executive with the largest budget…: Budget size is not a sound decision rule.
• Approve every executive's favorite idea so…: Funding everything dilutes resources.

Key takeaway: Use shared criteria to prioritize AI ideas across leaders.

stem: A company asks when AI creates only a temporary advantage. Which situation fits best?

choices.text: When the capability depends on specialized expert knowledge captured in the company's own processes
When the capability is built on years of proprietary operational data and embedded in core workflows
When the capability improves continuously from customer feedback that only this company collects
When the capability relies on widely available tools and public data that competitors can adopt quickly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Advantages built on commodity tools and public data are easy to replicate. Proprietary data, expertise, and feedback loops are harder to copy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• When the capability depends on specialized…: Captured expertise is hard to copy.
• When the capability is built on years of…: Proprietary data embedded in workflows is durable.
• When the capability improves continuously…: Unique feedback loops compound over time.

Key takeaway: Advantages from commodity AI are temporary; proprietary assets make them last.

stem: A company introduced an AI tool that drafts marketing emails. Which metric best captures quality alongside efficiency?

choices.text: The number of different templates the tool can produce when asked for new variations of an email
The average character count of generated emails compared with emails written in previous campaigns
Email engagement rates, such as click-through and conversion, compared with human-written emails
The number of emails the tool generates each hour compared with the number marketers write by hand

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Engagement and conversion show whether the emails work, complementing efficiency measures such as drafting time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of different templates the tool…: Variety of templates is not an outcome.
• The average character count of generated…: Length says nothing about effectiveness.
• The number of emails the tool generates each…: Volume is an efficiency or activity measure.

Key takeaway: Measure AI content by the outcomes it drives, not by how much is produced.

stem: A recruiting chatbot answers candidates' questions. Leadership wants to be sure it treats all candidates fairly. Which practice best supports this?

choices.text: Test responses with varied candidate profiles and compare tone and content across groups
Remove all candidate names from the chat window so the chatbot never sees anyone's identity at all
Limit the chatbot to one answer per question so that every candidate always receives an identical reply
Rely on the vendor's statement that the model is unbiased, since vendors test models before release

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fairness should be tested in the actual use: systematically comparing responses for varied profiles reveals disparities that vendor claims cannot rule out.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all candidate names from the chat…: Hiding names does not remove other signals of identity.
• Limit the chatbot to one answer per question…: Identical short replies reduce usefulness and do not prove fairness.
• Rely on the vendor's statement that the…: Vendor testing does not cover this company's use and prompts.

Key takeaway: Test fairness in your own use case with varied, representative inputs.

stem: A company's AI policy commits to 'robustness.' Which practice best demonstrates it?

choices.text: Choosing the largest model available, since larger models are guaranteed to be more robust in production
Testing the system with unusual, noisy, and adversarial inputs and confirming it behaves safely
Publishing the system's source code on a public repository so anyone can inspect its logic
Reporting the system's monthly usage statistics to the board as part of the company's quarterly review

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Robustness means reliable, safe behavior under unexpected or hostile inputs, which is shown by testing edge and adversarial cases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Choosing the largest model available, since…: Size does not guarantee robustness.
• Publishing the system's source code on a…: Publishing code is transparency, not robustness.
• Reporting the system's monthly usage…: Usage statistics do not show behavior under stress.

Key takeaway: Robustness is proven by stress-testing with unusual and adversarial inputs.

stem: A company operates AI systems in several countries with different AI regulations. Which approach best manages compliance?

choices.text: Apply only the rules of the country where the company's headquarters is located to all of its AI systems worldwide
Wait for a single global AI law to be passed before assessing any of the company's AI systems
Let each engineering team interpret the regulations independently without any central oversight
Maintain an inventory of AI systems with their risk level and the regulations that apply in each market

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An inventory that maps systems to risk levels and applicable regulations lets the company apply the right controls in each market.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Apply only the rules of the country where…: Operating in a market means its rules apply there.
• Wait for a single global AI law to be passed…: No single global law is imminent.
• Let each engineering team interpret the…: Independent interpretation leads to gaps and inconsistency.

Key takeaway: Govern AI with an inventory mapping each system to its risk and applicable laws.

stem: An internal audit finds nobody can say which foundation model version powered a customer-facing assistant three months ago. Which governance practice fixes this?

choices.text: Version and record the model, prompts, and configuration for each release, with change approvals
Ask the vendor to remember which model version the company was using during each past quarter
Delete old logs each month to reduce storage costs, since past versions are no longer relevant
Always use the newest model version automatically, so the question of versions never needs to arise

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Traceability requires recording what was deployed and when, including model version, prompts, and settings, under a change process.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ask the vendor to remember which model…: The company cannot rely on the vendor for its own audit trail.
• Delete old logs each month to reduce storage…: Deleting records removes evidence.
• Always use the newest model version…: Automatic upgrades make traceability worse and add unreviewed change.

Key takeaway: Track model, prompt, and configuration versions for every release.

stem: Attackers hide instructions in web pages that a company's research assistant summarizes, causing it to reveal internal notes. Which risk is this, and which mitigation helps?

choices.text: Model drift; retrain the assistant every month so that it learns to ignore instructions embedded in web pages
Data residency risk; move the assistant to a Region closer to the websites it summarizes most often
Indirect prompt injection; treat retrieved content as untrusted and filter it with prompt-attack detection
Latency risk; add caching so the assistant reads each web page only once instead of repeatedly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instructions hidden in content the model reads are indirect prompt injection. Treating that content as untrusted data and scanning it for attack patterns reduces the risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model drift; retrain the assistant every…: This is manipulation, not drift.
• Data residency risk; move the assistant to a…: Location does not affect injected instructions.
• Latency risk; add caching so the assistant…: Caching does not remove malicious instructions.

Key takeaway: Treat retrieved content as untrusted input and filter it.

stem: A company's AI assistant can access customer records. Which control most directly limits the damage if the assistant is misused?

choices.text: Store the assistant's credentials in its prompt so developers can see them easily
Allow the assistant to share its credentials with other applications that request them
Give the assistant administrator access so it never fails because of missing permissions
Grant the assistant access only to the data and actions its tasks require

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Least privilege limits what can be accessed or changed if the assistant is manipulated or makes a mistake.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Store the assistant's credentials in its…: Credentials in prompts can be leaked.
• Allow the assistant to share its credentials…: Sharing credentials widens exposure.
• Give the assistant administrator access so…: Broad access maximizes potential damage.

Key takeaway: Apply least privilege to AI systems just as to people.

stem: Which situation most requires human oversight of an AI system's outputs?

choices.text: Recommending a background color for a slide presentation
Deciding whether to deny someone a loan or insurance claim
Suggesting a subject line for an internal team newsletter
Sorting product photos into folders for an internal catalog

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Decisions with significant consequences for individuals, such as credit or claims, call for meaningful human review and the ability to contest the outcome.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recommending a background color for a slide…: Cosmetic and low risk.
• Suggesting a subject line for an internal…: Low-stakes and easily corrected.
• Sorting product photos into folders for an…: Internal and easily fixed.

Key takeaway: The higher the impact on people, the stronger the human oversight needed.

stem: A company wants a simple way to decide how much review each new AI use case needs. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Require the same full legal and ethics review for every AI use case, regardless of its impact or data
Skip review for any use case that uses a well-known foundation model from a major provider
Assign risk tiers based on impact and data sensitivity, with stronger review for higher tiers
Review only use cases proposed by the IT department, since other teams rarely use AI tools

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Risk tiering focuses scrutiny where impact and sensitivity are highest, keeping low-risk work moving.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Require the same full legal and ethics…: Uniform heavy review slows everything without improving outcomes.
• Skip review for any use case that uses a…: Model popularity does not determine risk.
• Review only use cases proposed by the IT…: Business teams use AI too.

Key takeaway: Scale governance to risk with tiered reviews.

stem: A retailer's AI assistant recommends products and can apply discounts. A customer tricks it into applying a 90% discount. Which TWO controls would have prevented this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Raising the model temperature so the assistant is less predictable to people trying to game it
Letting the assistant decide discount limits based on how loyal the customer seems in chat
A friendlier system prompt asking the assistant to be careful with discounts for customers
Guardrails and input filtering that detect attempts to manipulate the assistant's instructions
Business rules that cap discounts outside the model, regardless of what the model requests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Hard limits enforced outside the model cannot be talked around, and manipulation detection reduces the chance of successful prompt attacks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Raising the model temperature so the…: Randomness does not prevent manipulation and harms quality.
• Letting the assistant decide discount limits…: Model-decided limits are exactly what was exploited.
• A friendlier system prompt asking the…: Instructions alone can be overridden by manipulation.

Key takeaway: Enforce critical limits outside the model and detect manipulation attempts.

stem: A health insurer uses AI to prioritize claims for review. Which TWO practices best support accountability? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Remove the appeals process, since AI prioritization is more consistent than people
Keep records of decisions and the factors behind them for audit and appeal
Let the model's vendor decide how claims are prioritized without internal review
Keep the prioritization logic confidential from internal auditors to protect it
Name an accountable owner for the system and its outcomes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Accountability requires a clear owner and a record that lets decisions be explained, audited, and challenged.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove the appeals process, since AI…: Appeals are essential when decisions affect people.
• Let the model's vendor decide how claims are…: Delegating decisions to a vendor removes internal accountability.
• Keep the prioritization logic confidential…: Auditors need access to evaluate the system.

Key takeaway: Accountable AI needs a named owner and an auditable decision record.

stem: A board member asks what 'AI governance' means for the company. Which description is most accurate?

choices.text: The policies, roles, and processes that guide how AI is chosen, built, used, and monitored
The marketing plan that explains the company's AI capabilities to customers and investors
The technical process of training models on larger datasets to improve their accuracy scores
The procurement process for buying cloud computing capacity for AI workloads each year

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AI governance covers the policies, accountability, and oversight processes across the AI lifecycle.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The marketing plan that explains the…: Marketing communicates, it does not govern.
• The technical process of training models on…: Training is a technical activity, not governance.
• The procurement process for buying cloud…: Procurement is one input, not governance itself.

Key takeaway: Governance = policies, roles, and processes across the AI lifecycle.

stem: A company wants to use customer support transcripts to improve an AI assistant. The transcripts contain names, phone numbers, and card details. Which step should come first?

choices.text: Use the raw transcripts as they are, since the assistant is only for internal staff use
Detect and remove or mask personal and payment data before using the transcripts
Keep the transcripts forever so the assistant can learn from as much history as possible
Publish the transcripts internally so every employee can help review the assistant's quality

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sensitive personal and payment data should be removed or masked before reuse, reducing privacy and compliance risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use the raw transcripts as they are, since…: Internal use does not remove privacy obligations.
• Keep the transcripts forever so the…: Indefinite retention conflicts with data minimization.
• Publish the transcripts internally so every…: Wider access increases exposure.

Key takeaway: Minimize and mask sensitive data before using it for AI.

stem: A company plans to use AI to generate product images that include people. Which responsible AI consideration is most relevant?

choices.text: Selecting an image format that compresses well for email marketing campaigns
Making sure every generated image uses the company's standard corporate fonts and font sizes
Choosing the image resolution that loads fastest on older mobile phone browsers
Representing diverse people fairly and avoiding stereotypes in the generated images

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Generated images of people can reinforce stereotypes or exclude groups; reviewing for fair and diverse representation is a core responsible AI concern.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Selecting an image format that compresses…: Format is a technical detail.
• Making sure every generated image uses the…: Fonts are a brand detail.
• Choosing the image resolution that loads…: Resolution is a performance detail.

Key takeaway: Check generated content for fair representation and stereotypes.

stem: A company debates whether to disclose AI use in customer-facing decisions. Legal says disclosure is not required in one market. Which approach best reflects responsible AI leadership?

choices.text: Stop using AI in that market to avoid having to make any decision about disclosure
Never disclose AI use unless a regulator specifically requires it in that market
Disclose AI use where it meaningfully affects customers, even where not legally required
Disclose AI use only after a customer complains about a decision they received

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Responsible practice goes beyond minimum legal requirements where transparency affects trust and people's ability to understand decisions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop using AI in that market to avoid having…: Abandoning value avoids the question rather than addressing it.
• Never disclose AI use unless a regulator…: Minimum compliance can erode trust.
• Disclose AI use only after a customer…: Disclosing after complaints is reactive.

Key takeaway: Responsible AI can exceed legal minimums when trust is at stake.

stem: A company wants employees to use generative AI to boost productivity but worries about confidential data leaking into public tools. Which approach best balances both goals?

choices.text: Provide approved enterprise AI tools with data protections, and publish clear usage guidance
Permit public tools only for executives, since executives handle less confidential information
Ban generative AI entirely until the company can guarantee that no data will ever be exposed
Allow any public AI tool, since employees are responsible for judging what is safe to share

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Approved tools with enterprise protections meet the productivity need safely, and clear guidance reduces risky behavior.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permit public tools only for executives,…: Executives often handle the most sensitive information.
• Ban generative AI entirely until the company…: A total ban pushes use underground and forgoes benefits.
• Allow any public AI tool, since employees…: Leaving it to individual judgment leads to leaks.

Key takeaway: Offer safe, approved AI tools rather than banning or ignoring AI use.

stem: A lending model performs well overall but has a much higher error rate for applicants with thin credit files. What should the governance review require?

choices.text: Approve the model, since the overall error rate meets the target set in the business case
Report only the overall error rate to regulators, since segment results are optional details
Exclude thin-file applicants from lending entirely so the model's errors no longer matter
Measure performance by applicant segment and address the gap before or alongside deployment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Aggregate metrics can hide poor performance for specific groups. Segment-level evaluation and remediation are key to fair and reliable lending.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Approve the model, since the overall error…: Meeting an overall target can mask harm to a group.
• Report only the overall error rate to…: Hiding segment results undermines accountability.
• Exclude thin-file applicants from lending…: Excluding the group shifts harm rather than fixing it.

Key takeaway: Evaluate AI by segment, not only in aggregate.

stem: Which TWO items should an AI governance policy define? (Select TWO)

choices.text: How AI systems are monitored and reviewed after deployment
The exact prompt wording every employee must use when asking questions
The specific GPU model the company will buy for all future AI projects
The color scheme required for every AI-powered internal application
Who approves new AI use cases and on what criteria

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Governance defines decision rights and criteria for approval, and ongoing monitoring and review after launch.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The exact prompt wording every employee must…: Prompt wording is operational detail.
• The specific GPU model the company will buy…: Hardware choice is a technical decision.
• The color scheme required for every…: Visual design is not governance.

Key takeaway: Governance sets approval rights, criteria, and post-deployment oversight.

stem: A sales VP hears that a lead-scoring model uses 'supervised learning.' Which description is accurate?

choices.text: The model is monitored by a supervisor who approves every score before it reaches the sales team
The model groups leads into clusters without being told which past leads actually converted
The model learned from past leads that were already labeled as converted or not converted
The model is retrained by the sales team every morning using a manual spreadsheet process

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Supervised learning trains on examples with known outcomes (labels), such as whether each past lead converted.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The model is monitored by a supervisor who…: Human approval is oversight, not the learning type.
• The model groups leads into clusters without…: Grouping without labels is unsupervised learning.
• The model is retrained by the sales team…: Retraining schedule is unrelated to the learning type.

Key takeaway: Supervised learning = learning from labeled examples.

stem: A retailer wants to discover natural customer segments without predefined categories. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Reinforcement learning that rewards the model each time a customer makes a purchase online
Unsupervised clustering that groups customers by similar purchasing behavior
Text generation that writes a description of each customer based on their account profile
Supervised classification that assigns customers to segments the marketing team defined last year

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Discovering groups without labels is an unsupervised task; clustering finds customers with similar behavior.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reinforcement learning that rewards the…: Reinforcement learning optimizes actions, not segments.
• Text generation that writes a description of…: Descriptions do not discover segments.
• Supervised classification that assigns…: Classification needs predefined labels.

Key takeaway: Use unsupervised learning to discover groups you have not defined.

stem: A manufacturer wants cameras on its production line to catch defective parts automatically. Which AI capability is needed?

choices.text: Natural language processing that reads the maintenance manuals for each machine
Speech recognition that listens to operators describing problems on the line
Recommendation systems that suggest spare parts to buy for the production line
Computer vision that classifies or detects defects in images of each part

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspecting images for defects is a computer vision task; services such as Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels support it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Natural language processing that reads the…: Reading manuals does not inspect parts.
• Speech recognition that listens to operators…: Speech is not the inspection input.
• Recommendation systems that suggest spare…: Recommendations do not detect defects.

Key takeaway: Visual inspection problems call for computer vision.

stem: A company wants a chatbot for employee IT questions. Answers must be fast and consistent for 50 common questions, and new questions are rare. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: A custom-trained large language model built from scratch for the company's IT help desk team
A fully autonomous agent with access to reset any system and change any user setting
A simple intent-based bot with approved answers, adding generative AI only if needs grow
No automation, since IT questions are too varied for any kind of chatbot to answer well

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For a small, stable set of questions, a rule- or intent-based bot with approved answers is cheaper, faster, and more predictable than a complex generative solution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A custom-trained large language model built…: Training a model from scratch is excessive.
• A fully autonomous agent with access to…: Broad autonomous access adds risk without need.
• No automation, since IT questions are too…: Fifty common questions are well suited to automation.

Key takeaway: Choose the simplest solution that meets the need; generative AI is not always required.

stem: A team says its assistant uses 'embeddings' to find related documents. What are embeddings, in business terms?

choices.text: Numeric representations of text that place similar meanings close together, enabling semantic search
Keywords that employees must tag on every document before the assistant can find it
Short summaries of each document written by the model for employees to skim quickly
Encrypted copies of documents stored inside the model so that nobody outside the company can read them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Embeddings convert content into vectors where similar meanings are near each other, so searches find related content even with different wording.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keywords that employees must tag on every…: Embeddings do not require manual tagging.
• Short summaries of each document written by…: Summaries are generated text, not embeddings.
• Encrypted copies of documents stored inside…: Embeddings are not encryption.

Key takeaway: Embeddings enable meaning-based search.

stem: A company's assistant must follow a strict response format so downstream systems can read it. Which approach improves format reliability most?

choices.text: Ask the model to be creative with formatting so that outputs look more natural to downstream systems
Give explicit format instructions with an example, and validate the output before passing it on
Raise the temperature so the model tries several formats and picks the best one on its own
Remove all formatting guidance so the model uses whatever structure it prefers for each answer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clear instructions and examples steer structure, and validation catches outputs that do not match before they break downstream systems.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ask the model to be creative with formatting…: Creativity undermines consistency.
• Raise the temperature so the model tries…: Higher temperature increases variation.
• Remove all formatting guidance so the model…: No guidance produces inconsistent output.

Key takeaway: Specify, demonstrate, and validate required output formats.

stem: Which statement about foundation models is accurate for business planning?

choices.text: They always know a company's internal information without being given any documents or data
They learn continuously from every user conversation and update their weights in real time automatically
They are built for one narrow task and cannot be applied to any other use without rebuilding them
They are trained on broad data and can be adapted to many tasks with prompting, retrieval, or fine-tuning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Foundation models are pre-trained broadly and adapted to many tasks. They do not automatically learn from each conversation or know private company data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• They always know a company's internal…: Internal data must be provided.
• They learn continuously from every user…: Deployed models do not update weights from each chat.
• They are built for one narrow task and…: That describes traditional task-specific models.

Key takeaway: Foundation models are broad and adaptable, but they do not know your data unless you provide it.

stem: A bank's data team says its model needs 'inference latency under 200 milliseconds.' Why does this matter to the business?

choices.text: Card payments are approved in real time, so fraud checks must finish before the transaction completes
Latency determines how accurate the model is, so faster models always catch more fraud cases
Regulators require every AI model in banking to respond in under 200 milliseconds by law
Lower latency reduces the amount of historical training data the model needs to learn fraud patterns well

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Some decisions happen in real time; if the model is too slow, it cannot be used in the transaction flow at all.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Latency determines how accurate the model…: Speed and accuracy are different properties.
• Regulators require every AI model in banking…: There is no such universal legal requirement.
• Lower latency reduces the amount of…: Latency does not affect training data needs.

Key takeaway: Latency requirements come from where the decision happens in the business process.

stem: A publisher wants to translate articles into five languages quickly while keeping brand terminology consistent. Which TWO elements best support this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Speech synthesis to read each article aloud before translation begins for reviewers
Sentiment analysis to decide which articles should be translated into which languages
Human review of high-visibility articles before they are published in each language
Image classification to label the photos in each article before translating the text
Machine translation with a custom terminology list for brand and product terms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Custom terminology keeps brand terms consistent in machine translation, and human review of important content catches nuance and quality issues.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Speech synthesis to read each article aloud…: Speech synthesis does not help translation.
• Sentiment analysis to decide which articles…: Sentiment does not decide translation needs.
• Image classification to label the photos in…: Image labels do not translate text.

Key takeaway: Combine machine translation, terminology control, and targeted human review.

stem: A company plans several generative AI use cases but has no process for keeping documents current and approved. Which readiness gap matters most?

choices.text: The corporate font standard, since answers must match the company's brand typography
Content governance, since answers will only be as reliable as the documents the assistant draws on
Screen resolution of employee laptops, since the assistant's answers may be hard to read on them
Office seating layout, since teams using the assistant should sit near the data science team

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Assistants that retrieve company content inherit its quality; outdated or unapproved documents lead to wrong answers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The corporate font standard, since answers…: Typography is cosmetic.
• Screen resolution of employee laptops, since…: Display resolution is unrelated to answer quality.
• Office seating layout, since teams using the…: Seating does not affect reliability.

Key takeaway: For retrieval-based AI, content governance is a core readiness requirement.

stem: Which TWO questions best assess whether an organization is ready to launch its first AI use case? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Does every employee already know how to build machine learning models?
Has the company announced the initiative publicly to its customers and investors?
Is the required data available, of sufficient quality, and legally usable?
Has the company chosen a name for the AI center of excellence it may create?
Is there an executive sponsor and a business owner accountable for results?

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Usable data and clear sponsorship and ownership are fundamental preconditions for delivering and sustaining an AI use case.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Does every employee already know how to…: Not every employee needs to build models.
• Has the company announced the initiative…: Public announcements are not preconditions.
• Has the company chosen a name for the AI…: Naming is not readiness.

Key takeaway: Readiness starts with usable data and accountable ownership.

stem: A company rolls out an AI writing assistant. Which change management practice most improves adoption?

choices.text: Send one company-wide email announcing the tool and then provide no further support
Keep the rollout secret until everyone has been trained, to avoid early criticism
Require usage quotas and publicly list employees who do not meet them each week
Show teams concrete examples of how the tool helps with their own daily tasks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Adoption grows when people see relevant value in their own work; role-specific examples make benefits concrete.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Send one company-wide email announcing the…: One announcement without support rarely changes habits.
• Keep the rollout secret until everyone has…: Secrecy prevents engagement and feedback.
• Require usage quotas and publicly list…: Quotas and shaming breed resentment.

Key takeaway: Show people how AI helps their own work.

stem: A company scaled an AI assistant to all regions, but results vary widely between offices. What should leadership do first?

choices.text: Compare how offices use the tool and share the practices of high-performing offices
Stop measuring results by office, since variation between offices is always random noise
Assume the model performs differently by region and retrain it separately for each office
Remove the tool from the lower-performing offices immediately without investigating

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Variation often reflects differences in process, training, or use. Understanding and spreading what works is the quickest improvement.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop measuring results by office, since…: Ignoring variation hides improvement opportunities.
• Assume the model performs differently by…: Retraining assumes a model issue without evidence.
• Remove the tool from the lower-performing…: Removing it without analysis wastes potential value.

Key takeaway: When scaled results vary, learn from the best adopters before changing the technology.

stem: A company wants to experiment with AI quickly but its security team takes months to approve new tools. Which approach balances speed and control?

choices.text: Move experiments to employees' personal cloud accounts so the security team does not need to be involved at all
Create a pre-approved sandbox with guardrails and synthetic or non-sensitive data for fast experiments
Stop all experimentation until the security team finishes approving every possible AI tool
Let teams use any external tool with production data, since experiments are only temporary work

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A governed sandbox with safe data lets teams move quickly while staying within agreed controls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Move experiments to employees' personal…: Personal accounts bypass controls entirely.
• Stop all experimentation until the security…: A full stop sacrifices learning.
• Let teams use any external tool with…: Production data in unapproved tools creates serious risk.

Key takeaway: Enable fast, safe experimentation with governed sandboxes.

stem: A company runs a document-summary feature on the largest available model. Tests show a smaller model produces summaries users rate as equally good at one-fifth the cost. What should the product owner do?

choices.text: Use both models on every request and show users two summaries so they can pick the one they prefer
Switch the feature to the smaller model and keep monitoring quality ratings after the change
Keep the largest model, since the biggest model always gives the business the most value per request
Remove the summary feature, since any feature running on a foundation model is too expensive to justify

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When quality is equal for the task, the cheaper model delivers the same value at lower cost. Monitoring confirms quality holds in production.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use both models on every request and show…: Running both doubles cost and burdens users.
• Keep the largest model, since the biggest…: Larger models cost more and are not always better for a given task.
• Remove the summary feature, since any…: The smaller model makes the feature affordable.

Key takeaway: Match model size to the task; bigger is not automatically better value.

stem: Finance cannot tell which business unit drives the company's growing generative AI bill. Which practice gives the clearest cost attribution?

choices.text: Divide the total bill equally across all business units at the end of each month
Ask each business unit to estimate its own AI usage in a quarterly survey form
Tag AI resources and usage by business unit and report costs with those tags
Charge the entire AI bill to the IT department, since IT manages the cloud account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Consistent tagging lets cost reports split spending by owner, which supports accountability and informed decisions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Divide the total bill equally across all…: Equal splits ignore actual usage.
• Ask each business unit to estimate its own…: Estimates are unreliable.
• Charge the entire AI bill to the IT…: Central charging hides who drives costs.

Key takeaway: Tag AI spending by owner to make costs visible and accountable.

stem: A company's AI feature has steady, predictable high volume every day. The team pays standard on-demand model rates. Which option could lower cost?

choices.text: Keep paying on-demand rates, since commitments never reduce costs for predictable workloads
Move the workload to the most expensive model tier available, since higher tiers usually include automatic volume discounts
Reduce the feature's usage by turning it off every other day to cut the monthly bill in half
Commit to reserved or provisioned capacity sized to the steady volume, if the discount outweighs the commitment

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Predictable, sustained usage is where commitment-based pricing typically reduces unit cost; the decision should compare the discount to the commitment risk.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep paying on-demand rates, since…: Commitments often reduce cost for steady use.
• Move the workload to the most expensive…: Higher tiers usually cost more.
• Reduce the feature's usage by turning it off…: Turning the feature off removes value.

Key takeaway: Commit to capacity only for steady, predictable AI workloads.

stem: A company wants to find its best AI opportunities. Which discovery approach is most effective?

choices.text: Run workshops with business teams to map pain points, then assess which ones AI can address
Ask the vendor with the largest marketing budget which AI products the company should purchase
Copy the AI use cases announced by the three largest companies in any unrelated industries
List every AI capability that exists and try to apply each one somewhere in the organization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Starting from real business problems, identified with the people who own them, surfaces opportunities with genuine value and adoption potential.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ask the vendor with the largest marketing…: Vendors optimize for their own products.
• Copy the AI use cases announced by the three…: Other industries' use cases may not fit.
• List every AI capability that exists and try…: Technology-first searches produce solutions without problems.

Key takeaway: Discover AI opportunities from business pain points, not from technology lists.

stem: A company debates being first to market with a generative AI feature versus waiting to learn from competitors. When is moving first most justified?

choices.text: When early user feedback and data will compound into an advantage competitors cannot easily catch up to
When the feature relies entirely on public data and commodity tools that any competitor can adopt and use equally well
When the company has no clear use for the feature but wants to appear innovative in the press
When regulators have announced that the feature will soon be banned in the company's main markets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
First-mover advantage is real when early learning, data, and relationships build on each other. Without such a loop, fast followers often do better.

Why the other options are wrong:
• When the feature relies entirely on public…: Commodity features are easily copied, so being first gives little lasting edge.
• When the company has no clear use for the…: Appearance without purpose wastes resources.
• When regulators have announced that the…: Regulatory bans make the feature a poor investment.

Key takeaway: Move first only when early data or feedback creates compounding advantage.

stem: A marketing agency uses generative AI to create client campaigns. Which issue should be clarified before delivering AI-generated assets to clients?

choices.text: Whether the model's vendor has offices in the same city as the agency's biggest client
Ownership and usage rights for the generated content under the tools' terms and the client contract
How many images the model can generate per minute on the agency's current subscription plan and tier
Which web browser the designers use when reviewing the generated images on their laptops

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clients need clarity on who owns AI-generated work and how it may be used; this depends on tool terms and contracts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whether the model's vendor has offices in…: Vendor office location does not affect rights.
• How many images the model can generate per…: Throughput is operational.
• Which web browser the designers use when…: Browser choice is irrelevant.

Key takeaway: Clarify ownership and usage rights for AI-generated deliverables.

stem: A company has built separate AI solutions in five departments, each with its own tools and data pipelines. Costs are rising and lessons are not shared. Which strategic move helps most?

choices.text: Stop all departmental AI work and centralize every AI decision in one executive
Require each department to use a different vendor so they compete with each other
Merge all five departments into one so that only one AI solution is needed
Establish shared AI platforms and reusable components that departments build on

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A shared platform with reusable components reduces duplication and cost and spreads good practices, while still letting departments build solutions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop all departmental AI work and centralize…: Halting work and centralizing all decisions creates a bottleneck.
• Require each department to use a different…: Forced vendor variety increases fragmentation.
• Merge all five departments into one so that…: Reorganizing the company is disproportionate.

Key takeaway: Shared AI platforms reduce duplication and speed up reuse.

stem: Which metric best shows the customer-experience impact of an AI support assistant?

choices.text: The number of lines of code written to integrate the assistant with the company's CRM system
The assistant's average response length compared with human agents' replies
Customer satisfaction and resolution rates for conversations the assistant handles
The number of meetings the project team held while building the assistant

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Satisfaction and resolution capture whether customers were actually helped, which is the experience outcome.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The number of lines of code written to…: Code volume measures effort.
• The assistant's average response length…: Response length is not experience quality.
• The number of meetings the project team held…: Meetings measure activity.

Key takeaway: Customer experience impact is measured by satisfaction and resolution.

stem: A company's AI initiative has spent $2 million and results are poor. Managers argue it must continue 'because we have already invested so much.' How should leadership decide?

choices.text: Double the budget immediately, since more spending always improves poor AI results
Decide based on expected future costs and benefits, not on money already spent
Continue funding at any cost, since stopping would waste the $2 million already invested
Blame the vendor publicly and continue the project unchanged with the same plan

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Money already spent cannot be recovered; the decision should weigh only future costs against future benefits. Avoiding the sunk cost fallacy prevents further losses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Double the budget immediately, since more…: Spending more does not fix a flawed approach.
• Continue funding at any cost, since stopping…: This is the sunk cost fallacy.
• Blame the vendor publicly and continue the…: Blame does not change the economics.

Key takeaway: Ignore sunk costs; decide on future costs and benefits.

stem: A company evaluates AI vendors. Which TWO criteria best indicate long-term fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The vendor's number of social media followers compared with other AI vendors
The vendor's willingness to promise 100% accuracy in its sales presentation
Evidence of results with similar use cases and a realistic roadmap for the product
The vendor's office design and the quality of its conference room technology
Ability to meet the company's security, compliance, and data residency requirements

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compliance fit determines whether the solution can be used safely, and proven results plus a credible roadmap indicate the vendor can deliver over time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The vendor's number of social media…: Social media reach does not indicate fit.
• The vendor's willingness to promise 100%…: Promises of 100% accuracy are a red flag.
• The vendor's office design and the quality…: Office design is irrelevant.

Key takeaway: Evaluate AI vendors on compliance fit and proven, relevant results.

stem: A company sets objectives and key results for its AI program. Which key result is well formed?

choices.text: Become the most innovative company in the industry through artificial intelligence
Launch several exciting AI pilots that generate positive internal feedback
Use AI in as many processes as possible across the organization this year
Reduce average claims processing time from 10 days to 6 days by year end

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Good key results are specific, measurable, and time-bound, with a baseline and target.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Become the most innovative company in the…: Aspirational and not measurable.
• Launch several exciting AI pilots that…: Vague and measures sentiment, not outcomes.
• Use AI in as many processes as possible…: Vague and not tied to an outcome.

Key takeaway: Key results should be specific, measurable, and time-bound.

stem: A company rolled out an AI coding assistant and developer output rose, but defects in production also rose. What does this suggest about value measurement?

choices.text: Productivity gains must be weighed against quality costs, so defect rates belong in the KPIs
Defects are unrelated to development tools, so the increase must have a completely different cause
The assistant should be removed immediately, since any increase in defects cancels all benefits
Developer output is the only metric that matters, so the defect increase can be ignored safely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Higher output with more defects may reduce net value. Including quality metrics shows the full picture and guides controls such as review practices.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Defects are unrelated to development tools,…: The timing suggests a link that should be examined.
• The assistant should be removed immediately,…: The tool may still be net positive with better review practices.
• Developer output is the only metric that…: Ignoring defects overstates value.

Key takeaway: Pair productivity metrics with quality metrics.

stem: A company wants to differentiate its customer service with AI. Which approach is least likely to be copied by competitors?

choices.text: Train staff and AI together on the company's unique service processes and customer history
Announce the chatbot with a larger advertising campaign than any competitor can afford
Use a public foundation model with a generic prompt that any company could write easily
License the same off-the-shelf chatbot product that competitors are already using

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Combining unique processes, proprietary history, and trained people creates an experience that is hard to replicate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Announce the chatbot with a larger…: Advertising can be matched and does not improve service.
• Use a public foundation model with a generic…: Generic prompts are easy to copy.
• License the same off-the-shelf chatbot…: Identical products give no differentiation.

Key takeaway: Differentiate with proprietary processes and data, not common tools.

stem: A company must decide whether a use case even needs AI. Which TWO signals suggest AI is a good fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The company has no data related to the task and no way of collecting any in the future
Every output must be exactly reproducible and follow a published formula without any exception at all
The task involves patterns in large volumes of data that are hard to capture with explicit rules
The task happens once a year and takes a single employee about ten minutes to complete
Some errors are tolerable and can be caught by review or correction processes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AI fits when patterns are too complex for rules and when occasional errors can be managed. Exact, rule-defined, data-less, or trivial tasks rarely justify AI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The company has no data related to the task…: Without data, most AI approaches cannot work.
• Every output must be exactly reproducible…: Exact formula-driven tasks fit deterministic software.
• The task happens once a year and takes a…: The effort far exceeds the benefit.

Key takeaway: Use AI where patterns are complex and errors are manageable.

stem: A company estimates AI value using the vendor's case study from a much larger customer. What is the main risk?

choices.text: Larger customers always see smaller benefits, so this company will see much greater value
Results depend on context, so benefits may not transfer to this company's scale, data, and processes
The only risk is that the vendor may raise prices after the company signs the contract
Case studies are always false, so any vendor-reported results should be assumed to have zero value here

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Value depends on the organization's data, processes, and scale. Estimates should be grounded in the company's own baseline and ideally a pilot.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Larger customers always see smaller…: There is no rule that smaller companies gain more.
• The only risk is that the vendor may raise…: Pricing risk exists but is not the main issue with this estimate.
• Case studies are always false, so any…: Case studies can be informative, just not directly transferable.

Key takeaway: Ground value estimates in your own baselines and pilots.

stem: A company considers joining an industry consortium that shares anonymized data to train fraud models. Which consideration matters most?

choices.text: Whether the consortium's logo will appear on the company's public website after the partnership is formally announced
Whether the consortium meets in person or online, since meeting format decides the value created
Whether competitors also join, since the company should only join groups its competitors avoid
Whether shared learning improves detection enough to outweigh losing some exclusivity of the company's data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Consortium data can improve models for everyone, but it reduces how unique the company's data advantage is. The decision weighs that trade-off, along with privacy terms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Whether the consortium's logo will appear on…: Logo placement is marketing.
• Whether the consortium meets in person or…: Meeting format does not determine value.
• Whether competitors also join, since the…: Competitor participation is often the point of such consortia.

Key takeaway: Weigh shared-data gains against the loss of data exclusivity.

stem: A product team says its churn model outputs 'a probability of 0.82' for a customer. How should account managers interpret this?

choices.text: Exactly 82% of the customer's active contracts will be cancelled, and the remaining 18% will be renewed automatically
The customer will definitely leave within 82 days unless the account manager offers a discount immediately
The model is 82% finished with its training and will produce final answers once training has completed
The model estimates a high likelihood of churn, not a certainty, so it should guide priority rather than decide alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model outputs are often probabilities. A score of 0.82 indicates high estimated risk, which should prioritize action, not replace judgment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Exactly 82% of the customer's active…: The number is a likelihood for the customer, not a split of contracts.
• The customer will definitely leave within 82…: A probability is not a certainty or a time frame.
• The model is 82% finished with its training…: The score is a prediction, not training progress.

Key takeaway: Treat model scores as probabilities that guide decisions, not certainties.

stem: A data science lead explains that the team holds back part of the data that the model never sees during training. Why?

choices.text: To test the model on unseen data and estimate how it will perform on real future cases
To keep sensitive records out of the model, since held-back data is automatically encrypted
To save storage costs, since keeping all of the data in training would require a larger bucket
To reduce the time needed for training, since smaller datasets are always more accurate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A held-out test set estimates how the model generalizes to new data, which is what matters in production.

Why the other options are wrong:
• To keep sensitive records out of the model,…: Holding data back does not encrypt it.
• To save storage costs, since keeping all of…: Storage cost is not the reason.
• To reduce the time needed for training,…: Smaller training sets are not always more accurate.

Key takeaway: Evaluate models on data they did not train on.

stem: A bank wants to automatically read handwritten and typed fields from loan application forms and verify them against its records. Which combination of AI capabilities fits?

choices.text: A recommendation model that suggests which loan product each applicant would most likely want to buy
Document extraction to read the fields, followed by rule-based checks against existing records
Speech recognition to capture each applicant reading the form aloud during a phone call
Image generation to recreate each form digitally, followed by manual retyping of every field

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Extraction turns documents into data, and deterministic checks verify that data against records, combining AI with rules where each fits best.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A recommendation model that suggests which…: Recommendations do not read or verify forms.
• Speech recognition to capture each applicant…: Speech is not the input.
• Image generation to recreate each form…: Generated images do not extract data.

Key takeaway: Combine AI extraction with rule-based verification.

stem: A streaming service wants to recommend shows and also explain to users why each show was suggested. Which approach best meets both needs?

choices.text: A translation model that converts the show catalog into the user's preferred language before suggesting
A random selection of popular shows, since users cannot tell how recommendations are chosen anyway
A recommendation model whose outputs are paired with explanations based on the user's viewing history
A text generation model that invents a reason for each suggestion without looking at viewing history

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Recommendations grounded in behavior, with explanations tied to that behavior, are both relevant and understandable to users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A translation model that converts the show…: Translation does not recommend or explain.
• A random selection of popular shows, since…: Random picks are not personalized.
• A text generation model that invents a…: Invented reasons are misleading.

Key takeaway: Pair recommendations with explanations grounded in real signals.

stem: A manager reads that a model's output is limited to '1,000 tokens.' What is a token?

choices.text: A small unit of text, such as a word or part of a word, used to measure model input and output
A prepaid payment voucher that the company must buy in advance before using any foundation model
A single complete document, so the model can return at most 1,000 documents per request
A security credential that proves a user is allowed to call the model's API endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tokens are chunks of text that models read and write; limits and pricing are usually expressed in tokens.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A prepaid payment voucher that the company…: Tokens are units of text, not vouchers.
• A single complete document, so the model can…: A token is far smaller than a document.
• A security credential that proves a user is…: That describes an authentication token, not a text token.

Key takeaway: Tokens are units of text that drive limits and cost.

stem: A company's assistant needs to use today's exchange rates, which change daily, in its answers. Which approach is most reliable?

choices.text: Include last year's exchange rates in the system prompt, since rates change only slightly over time
Have the assistant call a rates service at question time and use the returned values in its answer
Ask the model to estimate current rates from its training data, since models know recent market data
Fine-tune the model every day on the latest exchange rates so it memorizes the current values

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Live, frequently changing data should be fetched when needed, through a tool or API call, rather than relying on model memory or training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Include last year's exchange rates in the…: Old rates can be materially wrong.
• Ask the model to estimate current rates from…: Training data is dated and cannot know today's rates.
• Fine-tune the model every day on the latest…: Daily fine-tuning is costly and still lags.

Key takeaway: Fetch live data through tools; do not rely on model memory.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a multimodal model from a text-only model?

choices.text: A multimodal model supports several languages, while a text-only model supports only English text
A multimodal model can run in several AWS Regions, while a text-only model runs in one Region only
A multimodal model is always cheaper to use than a text-only model, regardless of the task at hand
A multimodal model can take in and reason over more than one kind of input, such as images and text

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multimodal models handle multiple input types, such as images plus text, enabling tasks like answering questions about a photo.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A multimodal model supports several…: Language support is a different property.
• A multimodal model can run in several AWS…: Regional availability is unrelated.
• A multimodal model is always cheaper to use…: Cost depends on model and usage.

Key takeaway: Multimodal = multiple input types, such as text and images.

stem: A company trained a model on data from 2020 to 2022. It is used in 2026 and performs worse each month. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Models always lose exactly one percent of accuracy per month regardless of changes in the data
The model's software license expired in 2023, which gradually reduces its accuracy each month
Customer behavior and conditions changed since training, so the model's learned patterns are outdated
The model is too accurate for 2026 data, so it needs to be made less precise to fit the current business needs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When the world changes, the data a model sees drifts from what it learned. Monitoring and retraining on recent data address this.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Models always lose exactly one percent of…: There is no fixed decay rate.
• The model's software license expired in…: Licenses do not change model accuracy.
• The model is too accurate for 2026 data, so…: Being too accurate is not the problem.

Key takeaway: Models age as the world changes; monitor and retrain.

stem: A retailer wants shoppers to search for products by uploading a photo of an item they like. Which AI capability enables this?

choices.text: Speech recognition that converts a shopper's spoken product description into text
Sentiment analysis of product reviews to find the items shoppers like the most overall
Visual similarity search that matches the uploaded image to catalog product images
Forecasting that predicts which products will sell best during the next season

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Image-based search compares visual features of the uploaded photo with catalog images to find similar items.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Speech recognition that converts a shopper's…: Speech is not the input.
• Sentiment analysis of product reviews to…: Sentiment ranks reviews, not visual similarity.
• Forecasting that predicts which products…: Forecasting predicts demand, not matches.

Key takeaway: Image-based product search relies on visual similarity.

stem: A company's generative AI assistant sometimes gives different answers to the same policy question. Which TWO changes improve consistency? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Lower the temperature setting for this use case
Increase the maximum output length for each response
Remove the system prompt so the model has fewer instructions
Switch to a model that has a larger image-generation capability
Ground answers in the same retrieved policy text each time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Lower temperature reduces randomness, and grounding in the same source text anchors the content of answers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the maximum output length for each…: Longer outputs do not improve consistency.
• Remove the system prompt so the model has…: Removing instructions tends to increase variation.
• Switch to a model that has a larger…: Image generation is unrelated.

Key takeaway: For consistent answers, reduce randomness and ground in the same sources.

stem: An executive asks how 'AI,' 'machine learning,' and 'deep learning' relate. Which answer is accurate?

choices.text: Deep learning is the broadest category, and AI is a narrow technique used only for image recognition
They are three unrelated technologies that happen to share similar marketing language from vendors
AI and machine learning are identical terms, while deep learning refers to storing data deep in long-term archives
Machine learning is a subset of AI, and deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AI is the broad field; machine learning learns from data; deep learning is machine learning with multi-layer neural networks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deep learning is the broadest category, and…: The hierarchy is reversed.
• They are three unrelated technologies that…: They are nested, not unrelated.
• AI and machine learning are identical terms,…: Deep learning is a learning method, not storage.

Key takeaway: AI ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning.

stem: A hospital wants AI to help radiologists by highlighting possible anomalies in scans. Which design principle is most appropriate?

choices.text: Show radiologists only the scans the AI marks as normal, so they can focus on routine cases
Use AI as decision support that flags findings for radiologists, who make the final diagnosis
Let AI make final diagnoses automatically, since models never tire and are always more accurate
Avoid AI entirely, since any tool that can make mistakes should never be used in healthcare

explanation:
Why this is correct:
In high-stakes domains, AI works best as an assistant that improves human decisions, with experts retaining final responsibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Show radiologists only the scans the AI…: Hiding flagged scans defeats the purpose.
• Let AI make final diagnoses automatically,…: Full automation removes necessary oversight and models do make errors.
• Avoid AI entirely, since any tool that can…: Assistive AI can improve outcomes when overseen.

Key takeaway: In high-stakes settings, use AI to support experts, not replace them.

stem: A company wants a model to classify support tickets into categories but has only a handful of labeled examples. Which approach can work quickly?

choices.text: Asking customers to classify their own tickets and removing any automated classification entirely
Waiting until the company collects one million labeled tickets before attempting classification
Few-shot prompting a foundation model with a small number of labeled examples in the prompt
Training a new deep learning model from scratch using only the handful of labeled examples

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Foundation models can perform classification from a few examples in the prompt, which works well when labeled data is scarce.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Asking customers to classify their own…: Self-classification is unreliable and burdens customers.
• Waiting until the company collects one…: Waiting forgoes value unnecessarily.
• Training a new deep learning model from…: A handful of examples is far too few to train from scratch.

Key takeaway: With few labels, try few-shot prompting before training.

stem: Which TWO data practices most improve a model's reliability? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Collecting as many unrelated datasets as possible to increase the data volume
Checking data for errors, duplicates, and missing values before training
Using only the most recent week of data to keep the dataset small and fast
Removing all rare cases so that the model focuses only on common examples
Making sure training data reflects the situations the model will face in use

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clean, representative data is the foundation of reliable models. Quantity without relevance or quality does not help.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Collecting as many unrelated datasets as…: Unrelated data adds noise.
• Using only the most recent week of data to…: One week is rarely representative.
• Removing all rare cases so that the model…: Rare cases often matter most.

Key takeaway: Quality and representativeness beat sheer volume.

stem: A company plans an AI tool that suggests salaries for new hires based on past offers. What is the main responsible AI concern?

choices.text: Hiring managers may prefer a different font on the page that shows salary suggestions
Salary suggestions will take too long to generate for hiring managers during interviews
The tool may use too much storage because salary records are usually very large files
Past offers may reflect historical pay gaps, which the model could learn and repeat

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Models trained on historical decisions can reproduce historical inequities. Pay data should be checked for gaps and outcomes monitored.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hiring managers may prefer a different font…: Presentation is cosmetic.
• Salary suggestions will take too long to…: Speed is not the main concern.
• The tool may use too much storage because…: Salary records are small.

Key takeaway: Historical decisions can encode bias that models will learn.

stem: A company's content moderation model can be tuned to catch more harmful posts at the cost of wrongly removing more legitimate posts. How should leadership approach the setting?

choices.text: Choose the balance deliberately based on the harms of each error type, and provide an appeal path
Let the model vendor pick the threshold, since vendors know best what each company's users need
Always maximize removal of harmful content, since wrongly removed posts have no real consequences
Always minimize wrongful removals, since harmful content is the users' own responsibility to avoid

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Both error types cause harm. Leadership should weigh them for the platform's context, set the threshold accordingly, and let people contest mistakes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Let the model vendor pick the threshold,…: The company is accountable for its own policy choices.
• Always maximize removal of harmful content,…: Wrongful removals harm users and trust.
• Always minimize wrongful removals, since…: Ignoring harmful content harms users and the platform.

Key takeaway: Set AI thresholds deliberately by weighing the harms of each error type.

stem: What is the purpose of an 'AI system inventory' in an AI governance program?

choices.text: To list the laptops, servers, and GPUs that the data science team uses for its model development work
To record which AI systems exist, their owners, purposes, and risk levels so they can be overseen
To track the office supplies purchased for the AI center of excellence each quarter
To catalog the AI conferences employees attended during the year for training budgets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An inventory gives governance visibility: what AI is in use, who owns it, what it does, and how risky it is.

Why the other options are wrong:
• To list the laptops, servers, and GPUs that…: Hardware lists are IT asset management.
• To track the office supplies purchased for…: Supplies are unrelated.
• To catalog the AI conferences employees…: Conference tracking is training administration.

Key takeaway: You cannot govern AI you have not inventoried.

stem: A company buys an AI product from a vendor for use in hiring. Which governance responsibility remains with the company?

choices.text: Only training recruiters on the product's interface, since fairness is purely a technical matter for the vendor
None, since the vendor is fully responsible for any outcomes produced by its AI product
Assessing and monitoring how the product performs and affects candidates in the company's own hiring
Only paying the vendor's invoices on time, since use of the product is the vendor's concern

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Organizations deploying AI remain accountable for its use and effects in their context, even when the product comes from a vendor.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only training recruiters on the product's…: Fairness in use is the company's responsibility too.
• None, since the vendor is fully responsible…: Accountability for use stays with the deployer.
• Only paying the vendor's invoices on time,…: Payment is not governance.

Key takeaway: Buying AI does not outsource accountability for how it is used.

stem: A company worries that its public-facing chatbot could be used to generate offensive content that is then shared with the company's brand attached. Which control most directly addresses this?

choices.text: Content filters on inputs and outputs that block harmful categories
A larger model, since larger models never produce offensive content
Limiting the chatbot to business hours so fewer people can use it for misuse
A disclaimer at the bottom of the page stating that the company is not responsible

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Filters applied to both prompts and responses block harmful content before it is shown, reducing brand and user harm.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A larger model, since larger models never…: Larger models can still produce harmful content.
• Limiting the chatbot to business hours so…: Hours limits reduce use but not misuse.
• A disclaimer at the bottom of the page…: Disclaimers do not prevent harm.

Key takeaway: Filter harmful content on both inputs and outputs.

stem: A company relies on a single AI vendor for a critical customer process. Which risk-mitigation step is most prudent?

choices.text: Assume the vendor's service will always be available, since large vendors never have outages
Move every other business process to the same vendor to simplify the vendor relationship
Avoid documenting the process so that competitors cannot learn how it works internally
Plan a fallback, such as a manual process or alternate model, and test it periodically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Critical processes need continuity plans. A tested fallback limits disruption if the AI service is unavailable or degrades.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Assume the vendor's service will always be…: All services can have outages.
• Move every other business process to the…: Concentrating everything increases dependency.
• Avoid documenting the process so that…: Missing documentation makes recovery harder.

Key takeaway: Plan and test fallbacks for critical AI dependencies.

stem: A mental health app uses AI to respond to users. Which safeguard is most important?

choices.text: Collect as much personal data as possible to personalize every response
Hide the fact that responses are AI-generated so users feel more comfortable
Make responses as long as possible so users feel the app is thorough and caring
Detect signs of crisis and route users to human help and emergency resources

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Vulnerable users in crisis need human support. Detecting risk and escalating is essential for safety.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Collect as much personal data as possible to…: Collecting excess data increases privacy risk.
• Hide the fact that responses are…: Hiding AI use undermines trust and informed use.
• Make responses as long as possible so users…: Length does not ensure safety.

Key takeaway: Protect vulnerable users with escalation to human help.

stem: Which TWO practices best prepare a company for regulatory audits of its AI systems? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Rely on employees' memories of how each system was built and tested in the past
Describe AI systems only in marketing materials and avoid internal documentation
Keep documentation of each system's purpose, data, testing, and risk assessments
Delete old model versions and logs promptly to minimize what auditors can request
Retain logs that show how systems behaved and which controls were active

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Audits require evidence: documentation of design and assessments, and logs showing how systems actually operated.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rely on employees' memories of how each…: Memory is unreliable and not auditable.
• Describe AI systems only in marketing…: Marketing is not evidence.
• Delete old model versions and logs promptly…: Deleting records undermines accountability and may breach obligations.

Key takeaway: Documentation plus operational logs make AI auditable.

stem: Which risk is most specific to AI agents that take actions, compared with assistants that only answer questions?

choices.text: Producing an answer that uses more words than necessary for the user's question
Taking an unintended real-world action, such as issuing a refund or deleting a record
Taking a few seconds longer to respond than a traditional web search would take
Responding in a formal tone when the user expected a more casual conversational tone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Agents that act on systems can cause real consequences, so action limits, approvals, and logging are critical.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Producing an answer that uses more words…: Verbosity is a minor quality issue.
• Taking a few seconds longer to respond than…: Latency is a performance issue.
• Responding in a formal tone when the user…: Tone is a style issue.

Key takeaway: Agents raise the stakes: errors become actions.

stem: A company publishes responsible AI principles but teams do not apply them. Which step best turns principles into practice?

choices.text: Embed the principles into checklists, review gates, and tools used during development and approval
Ask each employee to sign the principles once a year, without changing any of the development processes
Rewrite the principles in more inspiring language so that employees remember them more easily
Print the principles on posters and display them in every office meeting room and hallway

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Principles become practice when they are built into the processes and tools teams use, such as required reviews and checklists.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ask each employee to sign the principles…: Annual signatures do not create action.
• Rewrite the principles in more inspiring…: Better wording does not create compliance.
• Print the principles on posters and display…: Posters raise awareness but do not change process.

Key takeaway: Operationalize principles through processes and review gates.

stem: A company wants employees to know which AI tools are approved and how to use them safely. Which artifact serves this best?

choices.text: A spreadsheet of model benchmark scores collected from public leaderboards
A technical architecture document describing the network design of the data center
A press release about the company's AI investments sent to financial journalists
An acceptable use policy that lists approved tools, allowed data, and prohibited uses

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An acceptable use policy tells employees clearly what they may use, with which data, and what is prohibited.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A spreadsheet of model benchmark scores…: Benchmarks do not guide safe use.
• A technical architecture document describing…: Architecture documents serve engineers.
• A press release about the company's AI…: Press releases are external communication.

Key takeaway: Give employees a clear acceptable use policy for AI.

stem: A company can deploy an AI feature now with basic safeguards or wait three months to add stronger testing. The feature affects customer credit limits. Which choice is most responsible?

choices.text: Launch without safeguards, since customers can always call support if a credit limit is wrong
